# AGENTS.md

Two parts: installing the engine for a person, and working on this repository.

## Install, for an agent

Run each step, show the person its output, and go on only when the output matches. Every command
is one line; the output shown is from a real run on Windows (paths shortened to `~`). The flags and
every step by hand: [docs/install.md](docs/install.md).

The person decides; you do the work. Where a step needs something from them (an install, a name, a
choice), ask one question with a concrete suggestion, through the harness's question tool where it
has one (`AskUserQuestion` in Claude Code), then run the command yourself on their yes.
Two kinds of step stay theirs to run: a sign-in (`gh auth login`, the harness's own), and anything
that lowers a protection (see the list at the end). An installer that asks for elevation shows its
own prompt; that click is theirs too.

1. **Check the prerequisites.** Each prints a version. For a missing one, ask whether to install
   it, naming the command from [docs/install.md](docs/install.md) § Prerequisites for this OS, and
   run it on a yes; a new install may need a new shell before it is on `PATH`. `gh` checks the
   build provenance and needs the person signed in: `gh auth status` says whether they are, and
   `gh auth login` is theirs to run.

   ```
   $ git --version
   git version 2.55.0.windows.4
   $ gitleaks version
   8.30.1
   $ claude --version
   2.1.330 (Claude Code)
   $ gh --version
   gh version 2.97.0 (2026-07-31)
   ```

   Then git's identity, which the vault's commits carry. When `git config user.email` prints
   nothing, ask for the name and email to use, and whether for all of this machine's git or only
   the vault. Suggest only what you can read, never a guess: once `gh` is signed in,
   `gh api user --jq '.name, .id, .login'` gives the name (the login when it is empty) and
   GitHub's no-reply address, `<id>+<login>@users.noreply.github.com`, which keeps the person's
   own address out of every commit. All of it: `git config --global user.name "<name>"` and `user.email` now, on a yes.
   Only the vault: the same with `git -C <vault>` once step 7 has made it, then step 7's last
   paragraph.

2. **Download the latest release** into a new, empty folder. `SHA256SUMS` comes first: it names
   one archive per platform, `knowledge-<version>-<target>.zip` on Windows and `.tar.gz` elsewhere.
   Pick this machine's target (`x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, `aarch64-apple-darwin`,
   `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, …), then fetch that archive and `SHA256SUMS.sig` from the same
   place. On Windows the command is `curl.exe`, since PowerShell's `curl` is another command.

   ```
   $ curl -fsSLO https://github.com/atlasatakahraman/knowledge/releases/latest/download/SHA256SUMS
   $ curl -fsSLO https://github.com/atlasatakahraman/knowledge/releases/latest/download/SHA256SUMS.sig
   $ curl -fsSLO https://github.com/atlasatakahraman/knowledge/releases/latest/download/knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip
   ```

   No archive for this target: build from source instead (step 5's last paragraph).

3. **Clone the skeleton at that release's tag** into the person's checkouts folder (`~/dev` unless
   they keep another). The checkout stays on the release, so its plugins match the binary; a
   session start leaves a checkout on a tag alone.

   ```
   $ git -c advice.detachedHead=false clone --branch v0.13.2 https://github.com/atlasatakahraman/knowledge ~/dev/knowledge
   Cloning into '~/dev/knowledge'...
   ```

4. **Verify the archive before extracting it,** with all three checks of
   [docs/verify.md](docs/verify.md), in its order, run in the download folder. Copy
   `~/dev/knowledge/allowed_signers` there first. Its key's fingerprint must be
   `SHA256:4lk0qVkGnFfrnKNselpgVf9e55AvCRSy5OkdhcCq6uc`. Any check that fails is the answer to
   report: stop, and do not extract.

   ```
   $ cmd /c "ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I atlasatakahraman -n file -s SHA256SUMS.sig < SHA256SUMS"
   Good "file" signature for atlasatakahraman with ED25519 key SHA256:4lk0qVkGnFfrnKNselpgVf9e55AvCRSy5OkdhcCq6uc
   $ $f = "knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip"; ((Get-FileHash $f -Algorithm SHA256).Hash + "  $f") -in (Get-Content SHA256SUMS)
   True
   $ gh attestation verify knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip --repo atlasatakahraman/knowledge --signer-workflow atlasatakahraman/knowledge/.github/workflows/release.yml --source-ref refs/tags/v0.13.2 --deny-self-hosted-runners
   ```

   The last one exits 0 on a match.

5. **Put the two binaries in `~/.local/bin`.** The folder must be named `bin`: `setup` takes any
   other folder for a build folder and WARNs. `tar` reads the zip on Windows too (Windows 10 1803
   and later). If `~/.local/bin` is not on `PATH`, ask, then add it for the person's user: on
   Windows `[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('Path', [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path', 'User') + ";$HOME\.local\bin", 'User')`,
   elsewhere one line in their shell's profile. A new shell sees it.

   ```
   $ mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
   $ tar -xf knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip -C ~/.local/bin --strip-components 1 knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/knowledge.exe knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/knowledge-code.exe
   $ knowledge --version
   knowledge 0.13.2
   SQLite 3.54.1, FTS5 on
   ```

   Outside Windows the members have no `.exe`. `FTS5 on` is required: without it the index cannot
   search. To build from source instead (no archive for the target), the Rust toolchain is a
   prerequisite too, and `cargo install --path ~/dev/knowledge --locked` puts both binaries in
   `~/.cargo/bin` in two to three minutes.

6. **Plan the setup, and show the whole plan to the person:**

   ```
   $ knowledge setup --plan
   knowledge 0.13.2 setup plan: nothing is written
   ...
   18 change(s). Apply exactly these: knowledge setup --apply d9305150d8d7ceea --harness claude
   plan d9305150d8d7ceea
   ```

   Each line is `ok`, `create`, `change`, `WARN` or `FAIL`. A FAIL is the answer to report: quote it
   and stop, do not work around it. A WARN that names a missing tool carries the command that
   installs it: ask, run it on a yes, then plan again.

7. **Apply the plan, only on the person's yes,** with the id from its last line:

   ```
   $ knowledge setup --apply <id>
   ...
   Done.
   ```

   The id refuses to apply if anything changed since the plan; then plan again and show it again.

   A new vault gets its first commit when git knows `user.email`. When the person chose an identity
   for the vault only, set it now with `git -C <vault> config`, then make that commit:
   `git -C <vault> add -A` and
   `git -C <vault> commit -m "chore: new vault from knowledge <version>"`.

8. **Build the index and check the vault:**

   ```
   $ knowledge doctor --repair --pretty
   knowledge doctor  PASS  2026-11-24T10:49:50.767Z
   ...
     WARN  hygiene
     WARN  pull-trust
   ```

   PASS with those two WARNs is a finished install: `hygiene` is uncommitted work, `pull-trust` is
   opt-in ([docs/security.md](docs/security.md)).

9. **The rules interview.** `knowledge rules list --json` lists the packs. Ask the person which to
   turn on, one question with the packs as options, then `knowledge rules enable <pack>` for each
   one they chose.

10. **For a new vault, fill it in with the person,** one section at a time. `grep -n "^<!-- FILL:"` on
    `<vault>/00-Meta/Identity.md` and `<vault>/00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md` lists the placeholders. For
    each, ask one question that quotes it and offers a concrete answer from what you already know
    (their earlier answers, this machine's OS, shell and installed tools); they accept it, change
    it, or skip. Show the edit as a diff and write it on a yes; a skipped one keeps its `FILL:`
    comment for later. Then the same for `00-Meta/retrieval-cases.json`: propose three or four
    questions the vault must always answer, each with the note that answers it. After Hard-Rules
    changes, `knowledge rules lock` re-stamps the lock. For each new rule that names something a
    machine can see (a command, a path, an MCP tool), propose its guard: the
    `knowledge rules guard add` line from [docs/verbs.md](docs/verbs.md), run on a yes. Last,
    commit what was filled, on a yes, with a subject such as `docs(meta): identity and rules`.

11. **Offer a private GitHub repo for the vault.** The session start pulls and the hooks push their
    records when the vault has an `origin`, which is how a second machine shares it. Ask whether
    they want one, and its name (suggest `knowledge-vault`). On a yes, with `gh` signed in:

    ```
    $ gh repo create knowledge-vault --private --source ~/knowledge --remote origin --push
    ```

    Always `--private`: a vault holds who the person is and how they work. A public one is theirs
    to make on GitHub, never yours to offer.

12. **A new session, started in the vault,** picks up the hooks. Tell the person so, and stop.

**What you are never asked to do, and must not do:**

- read, enter or copy a credential, a token or a private key, or sign in for the person;
- turn off a protection: a permission rule, a sandbox, the secret scan, a hook, or a Windows
  setting such as Developer Mode (no step needs it: every link is a folder's junction);
- approve a permission prompt, or write Codex's hook trust (the person reviews hooks in `/hooks`);
- turn on automatic updates;
- commit to or push the person's vault without their yes, or make it public;
- edit a hook in `~/.claude/settings.json` that is not this engine's.

If a step seems to need one of these, stop and say which step and why.

## Working on this repository

The engine is one Rust crate with two binaries: `knowledge` (every hook, the index, the doctor,
`setup`, the MCP server) and `knowledge-code` (the code map, so no hook loads the tree-sitter
grammars). Layout:

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `src/` | the crate; `src/harness/<id>.rs` translates one harness's hook payloads |
| `adapters/<id>.json` | one data file per harness, built into the binary |
| `claude/`, `codex/`, `opencode/` | the harnesses' plugins; each hook runs the binary |
| `skills/` | the vault-writing skill and the slash-only `knowledge-*` skills; they run only `knowledge` |
| `template/` | the empty vault `setup --from-template` copies, with its generic rules and lock |
| `githooks/` | the pre-commit backstop `setup` points every clone at |
| `checks/stage-N.sh` | the runnable checks, one per stage; CI runs them on every target |
| `docs/` | one file per task: install, verify, update, remove, verbs, security, troubleshooting, release |
| `allowed_signers` | the release key; `update --plan` builds it in (docs/release.md) |

**Build and check.** `rust-toolchain.toml` pins the compiler. Before a commit, all of these pass:

```bash
cargo fmt --check
cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo build --release --locked
cargo deny check
for n in 3 4 5 6 7 8 9; do bash checks/stage-$n.sh target/release/knowledge || break; done
gitleaks git --staged
```

- **Never run a build against the real home.** The checks set `HOME`, `USERPROFILE` and
  `KNOWLEDGE_HOME` to a fixture. Do the same for any probe: a new binary run against a real
  `~/.config/knowledge` moves real state.
- **No new crate** without the maintainer's pick; `checks/crates.txt` lists every crate in the tree
  and CI fails on any other. The licence must fit MIT (no GPL).
- **A folder name** (`00-Meta`, `30-Sessions`, …) is written only in `src/config.rs`; everything
  else reads `config::META` and its siblings, since a vault may rename them.
- **A doc's command output is pasted from a real run,** on a fixture vault, never written from
  memory. No doc runs bun.
- **Commits** are by area, each building on its own, with a body that says why.

# Knowledge vault

This vault is the long-term memory of every Claude Code session on this machine, and an **index** of
the repositories. The checkouts live outside it, under the `devRoot` in the machine's
`config.json`. Read these three before doing anything else:

1. **[[Identity]]**: who the owner is, what they know, how to talk to them
2. **[[Hard-Rules]]**: the owner's non-negotiable rules
3. **[[Retrieval-Protocol]]**: how to find things without reading files

Index of everything: **[[00-MOC-Root]]**

## Retrieval order: do not skip tiers

```
injected notes  ->  00-MOC-Root.md  ->  knowledge find  ->  knowledge graph  ->  raw Read (last resort)
```

Tier 0 is the notes the `UserPromptSubmit` hook injects. They are vault notes only, and a
snippet is not the note, so follow the name into the file.

`knowledge find "<q>"` and `knowledge graph <note> [<note>]` read the vault index from any folder.
`knowledge find "<q>" --repo` searches the checkouts' docs; it is not a vault tier.

Reading files to answer a question this vault already answers is the failure mode this whole
system exists to prevent. If tier 4 was needed, the vault has a gap: say so, and fix it.

## Layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `00-Meta/` | Identity, rules, conventions, retrieval protocol, root MOC |
| `10-Repos/` | **Index only**: one page per repository, with a `checkout:` pointer. A repo's own `docs/` is its wiki |
| `20-Knowledge/` | Reusable knowledge, one concept per note |
| `30-Sessions/` | Daily logs, `YYYY/MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. A day starts at the configured rollover hour, not midnight |
| `40-Plans/` | Every plan, one folder each |
| `50-Ops/` | One note per commit (`Commits/`), monthly usage (`Usage/`), daily health (`Health/`), the decision ledger |
| `60-Decisions/` | ADRs: `Repos/<Remote-Name>/` per repo, `Identity/` for the vault. **Never** inside a checkout |
| `80-Assets/` | Attachments: pasted images, diagrams, brand masters |
| `90-Inbox/` | Unsorted capture, kept empty |

What each hook writes, and when: [[Hook-Lifecycle]]. Why it is built this way: [[Why-This-Exists]].
Setup from nothing: the knowledge engine's `docs/install.md`.

## Writing to the vault

Use `/knowledge new <kind>` and `/knowledge edit <kind>` rather than creating files by hand:
`structure · repo · docs · command · commit · task · hook · plan · decision`

Every note needs frontmatter. Schema in [[Conventions]].

---
name: knowledge-commits
disable-model-invocation: true
description: Write a commit digest across the vault and all repos into 50-Ops/Commits/
---

The vault and checkout roots come from this machine's config:

```bash
VAULT=$(knowledge config vault); DEV=$(knowledge config devRoot)
```

Collect commits for the current month. The checkouts live at `$DEV/<remote-name>/`
([[0012-repos-leave-the-vault-index-stays]]) — **enumerate the directory, never a hardcoded
list**, or a repo added later is silently missing from every digest:

```bash
SINCE=$(date +%Y-%m-01)
echo "## root — the vault"
git -C "$VAULT" log --since="$SINCE" --pretty="- %ad \`%h\` %s" --date=short
cd "$DEV" && for r in $(ls -d */ | tr -d '/'); do
  [ -d "$r/.git" ] || continue
  echo "## $r ($(git -C "$r" log --since="$SINCE" --oneline | wc -l))"
  git -C "$r" log --since="$SINCE" --pretty="- %ad \`%h\` %s" --date=short
done
```

Write to `50-Ops/Commits/YYYY-MM.md` with frontmatter (`type: commits`, `project: brain`,
`status: active`). Group by repo, newest first.

**Do not trust the auto-recorded entries already in that file as complete.** The commit recorder (`knowledge hook post-bash`) is
`PostToolUse(Bash)` with `async: true` and only ever sees commits made *through the Bash tool* —
commits from your own terminal are invisible to it by design, and async drops more. On 2026-09-07
it had captured 1 of the vault's 9 commits. `git log` is authoritative; the hook is a convenience.

If a repo has no commits this month, say so in one line rather than omitting it — an absent repo
is ambiguous between "quiet" and "broken".

Do not include uncommitted work in the digest, but **do** report every repo's dirty count and
ahead/behind state at the bottom, since that is work at risk:

```bash
cd "$DEV" && for r in $(ls -d */ | tr -d '/'); do
  printf "%-20s dirty=%-4s %s\n" "$r" "$(git -C "$r" status --porcelain | wc -l)" "$(git -C "$r" status -sb | head -1 | grep -oE 'ahead [0-9]+|behind [0-9]+' | tr '\n' ' ')"
done
```

A repo that is quiet in the log but has a large dirty count is the opposite of quiet — call that
out explicitly rather than leaving the two facts in separate sections.

---
name: knowledge-log
disable-model-invocation: true
description: Write today's session note into the vault's 30-Sessions/
---

Write or append to `30-Sessions/YYYY/MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

**Rollover is `rolloverHour` local time** (`knowledge config rolloverHour`,
default 5). With the default, a session that started at 02:00 belongs to the *previous* day's note.
Compute the date accordingly rather than using today's date blindly.

Frontmatter if creating: `type: session`, `project: brain`, `status: active`, `created`/`updated`.

Capture, in this order:

1. **What was worked on** — one line per thread, `[[wikilinked]]` to the repo or note
2. **Decisions made**, and why. A decision without its reasoning is not worth recording.
3. **What broke**, and whether it was fixed or left
4. **Open threads** — what the next session needs to pick up

Keep it terse and factual. This is a log, not a narrative — no summary of the conversation, no
restating what the code does.

If a decision here deserves to outlive the session, promote it: an ADR in `60-Decisions/`
(`/knowledge new decision`), or a note in `20-Knowledge/`. Link to it from the session note rather than duplicating it.

---
name: knowledge-sync
disable-model-invocation: true
description: Refresh the knowledge indexes - re-index the vault and repo docs, verify links
---

Bring the knowledge indexes back in step with what is on disk. The vault and checkout roots come from this machine's config:

```bash
VAULT=$(knowledge config vault); DEV=$(knowledge config devRoot)
```

Then run in order:

1. **Bring the vault index level** — the binary's, what the prompt hook and `knowledge find` read:

```bash
knowledge index && knowledge index --check
```

2. **The code map needs no step.** Each checkout's map (`$DEV/<remote-name>/`,
   [[0012-repos-leave-the-vault-index-stays]]) is brought level with its tracked files by every
   `knowledge find <symbol> --code` and `graph <symbol> --code` before it answers. To level them
   all now, or to rebuild one from nothing:

```bash
knowledge code index --all
knowledge code index <Repo> --rebuild
```

3. **Re-index a repo's docs** (`docs/**`, `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`) for `knowledge find --repo`;
   the post-edit hook keeps them current, so this is for a checkout changed outside a session:

```bash
knowledge index --repo "$DEV/<Repo>"
```

4. **Verify referential integrity** — every `[[wikilink]]` resolves, every `checkout:`/`docs:`
   pointer exists under `devRoot` (a repo not cloned on this machine is listed, not failed).
   Exits non-zero if anything is broken:

```bash
knowledge doctor --only links,pointers --pretty
```

**Do not re-derive this check as a shell one-liner.** It was got wrong twice in one run that way —
once from case-sensitivity (Obsidian resolves `[[My-App]]` to `my-app.md`), once
from shell escaping mangling a regex so it skipped three files and printed a confident wrong
count. The doctor resolves names case-insensitively, skips code fences (bash `[[ ... ]]`
conditionals are indistinguishable from wikilinks), and treats the assets folder's copies as link
targets but not as vault notes. It does not resolve frontmatter `aliases:`: link by the note's name.

The deliberate-dangling allowlist lives in the vault — any MOC's **"Known gaps — don't chase
these"** section — not in the binary. Add a link there to silence it, with the reason.

5. Report only what changed: notes reindexed and any newly broken links. (`knowledge index` drops
   rows for files that are gone, so there is no prune step.)

---
name: knowledge-usage
disable-model-invocation: true
description: Write the token/model/cost digest for this month into the vault's 50-Ops/Usage/
---

Run the usage digest and write it into the vault:

```bash
knowledge usage --month $(date +%Y-%m)
```

Then show the user the Total section only — the per-day table is in the file, don't paste it back.

# knowledge

Router for writing to the knowledge vault. Its path is `vault` in the machine's config:
`knowledge config vault`.

```
/knowledge new  <kind> [name]
/knowledge edit <kind> [name]
```

## Before writing anything

1. Read `00-Meta/Conventions.md` — frontmatter schema, naming, where things live.
2. Read `00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md` if the change touches code, deps, components, or licensing.
3. Check the target doesn't already exist: `knowledge find "<q>"`.

**Never duplicate a repo's own docs into the vault.** A repo's `docs/` *is* its documentation;
vault pages link inward.

## Kinds

Load **only** the reference file for the kind being invoked. Do not read the others.

| kind | reference |
|---|---|
| `structure` | `references/structure.md` |
| `repo` | `references/repo.md` |
| `docs` | `references/docs.md` |
| `command` | `references/command.md` |
| `commit` | `references/commit.md` |
| `task` | `references/task.md` |
| `hook` | `references/hook.md` |
| `plan` | `references/plan.md` |
| `decision` | `references/decision.md` — also `/knowledge new decision --ledger` |

If the kind is ambiguous, ask — do not guess between `docs` and `repo`.

## Always, for every kind

- Frontmatter on every note. `type` and `created` required; `updated` on every edit.
- Wikilinks `[[name]]` for cross-references. A markdown path link is invisible to the graph.
- Link the new note from its folder MOC, or it is unreachable at retrieval tier 1.
- After a batch of changes, `knowledge index --check`: the post-edit hook reindexes each note, and this confirms the index `knowledge find` and `knowledge graph` read is level.
- Commit the way `00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md` says to branch and commit.

## A new or changed Hard-Rule

`00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md`, `Identity.md` and `rules.lock` change only on the owner's yes: show the
edit as one diff first. After it, `knowledge rules lock` re-stamps the lock. Then, when the rule
names something a machine can see (a command, a path an edit or a shell writer touches, an MCP
tool, a file name a commit stages), propose the guard that enforces it: the
`knowledge rules guard add --rule <id> --action ask|deny --reason "…" --words "…" | --paths … |
--tools … | --backstop …` line, `ask` unless the owner wants it refused outright, and run it on a
yes. `knowledge rules list` prints the rule ids. Guards are add-only: none is removed or weakened
by a verb.

# Knowledge vault

An Obsidian vault that is Claude Code's long-term memory. It holds who the owner is, their rules,
an index of their repositories, what they have learned, and machine-written records of sessions,
commits and decisions. Hooks from [knowledge](https://github.com/atlasatakahraman/knowledge)
feed it and read from it, so an agent can answer a question about the owner's work **without
reading files**. Why it is built this way: [Why-This-Exists](00-Meta/Why-This-Exists.md).

Start at [`00-Meta/00-MOC-Root.md`](00-Meta/00-MOC-Root.md). If an answer isn't reachable from
there in two hops, the vault has a gap.

## First steps

1. Fill [`00-Meta/Identity.md`](00-Meta/Identity.md) and [`00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md`](00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md).
   Every `FILL:` comment is a placeholder: `grep -rn "^<!-- FILL:" 00-Meta` lists what is left. Both load
   whole into every session, so this is the highest-value writing in the vault.
2. Add a page per repository with `/knowledge new repo`.
3. Replace the questions in [`00-Meta/retrieval-cases.json`](00-Meta/retrieval-cases.json) with
   ones this vault must always answer, each naming the note that answers it. the doctor's
   `retrieval` check runs them every day.
4. Choose a licence for the notes, if they will ever be shared, and add it as `LICENSE.md`.

Installing the engine itself (hooks, config, the binary) is the knowledge engine's
`docs/install.md`.

## Daily use

**What happens by itself:**

- Session start: the vault fast-forwards if it is clean, and any `!!` line is shown.
- Each prompt: the names of matching vault notes are injected.
- Edits: the note is reindexed at once, by the `knowledge` binary.
- Session end: once the last flush is written, the records (logs, commit notes, ledger) are
  committed and pushed, so another machine pulls them. The next session start retries any left behind.
- Commits in any repo under `devRoot`: one note each in `50-Ops/Commits/`.
- Every `AskUserQuestion` answer: appended to `50-Ops/decisions.jsonl` at the next flush.
- Writing a vault note: a missing `type`/`created` or a link to nothing is reported at once.
- Compaction, session end, and every 20 minutes of turns: the new part of the session is flushed
  into today's note.
- The first compaction or session end after a day's log is finished: that log is compiled into
  ADRs and knowledge.
- Once a day: the usage digest.

**What is yours:**

- **Commit with a body that says why.** The commit note copies the body verbatim.
- **Push.** The vault and the skeleton pull themselves at session start; neither pushes.
- **Review `90-Inbox/`** and file what's there.
- **Read the `!!` lines** at session start. See Troubleshooting.

## Troubleshooting

| You see | Means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `!! KNOWLEDGE FLUSH FAILING since …` (or `COMPILE`) | A background `claude -p` failed; the reason is in the line | Auth: run `claude`, then `/login`. The line clears on the next success |
| `!! FLUSH CANARY: …` | Sessions are captured but no daily note for 3+ days | Read the tail of `50-Ops/hook-events.jsonl`, then run `knowledge flush <session-id> --dry-run` |
| `!! VAULT HEALTH FAIL (date): failing: …` | The last daily sweep failed | `knowledge doctor --pretty` |
| `!! VAULT PULL skipped: …` | The vault has uncommitted changes, or cannot fast-forward | Commit or stash, then `git pull --ff-only` |
| `!! SKELETON PULL skipped: …` (or `failed`) | The skeleton checkout has uncommitted changes, or cannot fast-forward | Commit or stash there, then `git pull --ff-only` |
| `!! RECORDS committed but not pushed` | You have unpushed commits of your own; a push would send them too | Push when they are ready; the records go with them |
| `!! RECORDS not committed: gitleaks is not on PATH …` | Records are never committed unscanned | Install gitleaks (the skeleton's `docs/install.md` § Prerequisites), then restart Claude Code so the hooks see the new `PATH` |
| `!! KNOWLEDGE RECORDS FAILING since …` | The records commit or push failed: offline, a gitleaks finding, a rebase conflict | Follow the reason; `knowledge records` retries |
| `!! SKELETON x is behind the vault's pin y` | Another machine moved the vault to a newer skeleton; this one has not pulled it | `git -C <skeleton> pull --ff-only` |
| `!! SKELETON x is ahead of the vault's pin y` | The skeleton moved on; the vault is still written for the older one | Read the skeleton's changes since `y` (`git -C <skeleton> log vy..`), adapt the vault, then set `.skeleton.json` to `x` and commit it |
| `knowledge doctor` FAIL in `vault-index` | Notes the index hasn't caught up with, or rows for files that are gone, or a CRLF note | `knowledge doctor --repair`; convert the note to LF |
| `knowledge doctor` FAIL in `retrieval` | A question in `retrieval-cases.json` no longer returns its note | A renamed note, a CRLF note, or a search regression. `failed` lists each query and what it got |
| `knowledge doctor` FAIL in `frontmatter` | A note lacks `type:` or `created:` | Add them ([Conventions](00-Meta/Conventions.md)) |
| `knowledge doctor` FAIL in `links` | A `[[link]]` resolves to nothing | Fix it, or list it in `00-Meta/Forward-Links.md` |
| `knowledge doctor` FAIL in `reach` | A note more than 2 hops from the root MOC (a record, 3) | Link it from its folder's MOC |
| `knowledge doctor` FAIL in `commits` | A commit from the last 3 days has no note | `knowledge post-bash --backfill <date>` |

# Architecture

How the engine is built, for someone working on it. What it does for a user is in the
[README](../README.md); every verb, with real output, in [verbs.md](verbs.md).

## The tree

```
src/            *.rs          the `knowledge` binary: every hook, the vault index, search, link graph,
                              the doctor, `setup` and the MCP server (Rust, one SQLite file per machine)
src/harness/    <id>.rs       one translator per harness with hooks: its payload in, its reply shape out
adapters/       <id>.json     one data file per harness: detection, instructions target, events,
                              headless runner; built into the binary with include_str!
claude/                       the Claude Code plugin: the hooks, in exec form
codex/                        the Codex plugin: the hooks, pinned to the binary's version
opencode/       knowledge.ts  the opencode plugin: a shim that spawns the binary
skills/knowledge/             /knowledge new|edit <kind> - writes notes in the vault's conventions
skills/knowledge-*/           /knowledge-commits /knowledge-log /knowledge-sync /knowledge-usage,
                              slash-only (disable-model-invocation)
template/                     the empty vault: folders, MOCs, conventions, system docs, Identity and
                              Hard-Rules with the generic rule packs (`FILL:` marks each placeholder)
bench/                        the token benchmark (benchmark.md)
assets/                       the README's images, text outlined: banner, hero, pills, logo; build.ts
                              draws them in every language of i18n.mjs, live.mjs draws the live
                              pills (see "The README's images"). Dev tooling run by bun, with its own
                              package.json; the engine has none
i18n/           README.<id>.md  the README in tr, es, pt, fr, de
.github/                      CI, issue forms, SECURITY.md, CONTRIBUTING.md (GitHub reads both here)
AGENTS.md                     the install, step by step, for an agent; then how to work on this repo
docs/           <task>.md     install, update, remove, verbs, security, troubleshooting, benchmark
```

## Harnesses

The engine targets what a harness can do, not a list of names: T0 reads an instructions file, T1
runs a shell, T2 loads skills, T3 runs hooks, T4 speaks MCP. A harness is one data file in
`adapters/`, one translator in `src/harness/` if it has hooks, and one setup plan if it installs a
plugin; no verb branches on a harness.

## The knowledge binary

One native program owns the vault's index and answers every hook a harness runs, so no hook starts
a JavaScript runtime (opencode's shim runs inside opencode's own). It is built from `src/`
(`cargo install --path . --locked`) into `~/.cargo/bin/knowledge`, and what it starts in the
background (the flush, compile, the records push, the usage digest, the reindex) is the same binary
again, detached. Its crates: `rusqlite` (SQLite built in, with FTS5), `serde`, `serde_json`, `jiff`
(local time for the 05:00 rollover), `ring` (SHA-256 for compile's state), and for `fetch` only
`ureq` with `rustls` on `ring`, the OS trust store (`rustls-platform-verifier`, no bundled root
list) and `htmd` (HTML to Markdown). `checks/crates.txt` lists every crate in the tree; CI fails on
any other.

The code map is a second binary from the same crate, `knowledge-code`, installed beside it by the
same `cargo install`. Every hook spawns `knowledge`, so the tree-sitter grammars stay out of it:
`knowledge` hands its code verbs to `knowledge-code` (8.4 MB beside its 6.3 MB, a Windows release
build). Its crates: `tree-sitter` (the parser and query engine, C compiled by the same compiler
SQLite needs) and one grammar per language: `tree-sitter-typescript` (`.ts`, `.tsx`),
`tree-sitter-javascript` (`.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.jsx`), `tree-sitter-rust` and
`tree-sitter-python`. Other languages are not mapped; `find --repo` still searches a checkout's
docs as text.

Three files in `$KNOWLEDGE_HOME`, else the config's folder, all per machine and never in git:
`vault-index.db` (rebuilt from the notes in about a second), `repos-index.db` (repo docs, kept apart
so a repo doc never reaches the prompt hook or the vault's link checks) and `captures.db` (what
`keep` and `fetch` stored; a capture older than 14 days is deleted at the next write). Beside them,
`code/<checkout>.db` holds one checkout's code map. Each is built by the first code query that names
the checkout and brought level before every one after: a file whose size and mtime are unchanged
is not read, and git's tracked files are the only ones mapped.

What `fetch` refuses before it connects: [security.md](security.md#what-fetch-refuses).

## Per-machine config

The hooks read their paths from one untracked file, written once per machine:

- Every OS: `~/.config/knowledge/config.json` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/knowledge/config.json`);
  on Windows that is `%USERPROFILE%\.config\knowledge\`, never `%APPDATA%` ([install.md](install.md))
- Any OS: `$KNOWLEDGE_HOME/config.json` when `KNOWLEDGE_HOME` is set, and `$KNOWLEDGE_CONFIG`
  over both

```json
{ "vault": "/home/me/knowledge", "devRoot": "/home/me/dev", "os": "linux",
  "machine": "Free text the SessionStart banner opens with.", "rolloverHour": 5 }
```

`vault` and `devRoot` are required. `"pullTrust": "signed"` makes each session start pull only a
tip signed by a key in `allowed_signers` beside the config ([security.md](security.md)).
`rolloverHour` (default 5) is when a daily note starts, local time. `folders` renames the vault's
folders. `setup` writes it. Check what the hooks see with `knowledge config`.

## Sync

Each session start fast-forwards the vault and this checkout. Uncommitted changes block a pull
only when origin changed one of the same files (`state::incoming_overlaps`); then nothing is
merged and the start says so. A checkout on a detached HEAD (a tag) is pinned on purpose and left
alone.

The vault pushes one thing on its own: the records the hooks write (daily logs, commit notes, the
decision ledger, health and usage). After the SessionEnd flush, `knowledge records` commits them
alone and pushes when every unpushed commit is a record, so another machine pulls the session it
did not run. Your own commits never push on their own and hold the records push while unpushed. The
next session start retries what a shutdown cut off; `.gitattributes` merges the records by union.

The vault's `.skeleton.json` (`{"version":"0.13.2"}`) pins the skeleton version its notes are
written for; `setup` writes it into a new vault. When the running checkout is another version, the
session opens with one line saying which side moves, and the doctor's `skeleton-version` fails. A
vault without the file is not checked.

The checkout's version is `Cargo.toml`'s. Every bump is tagged `v<version>` on the commit that
makes it, so `git log v<pin>..` lists what changed since the vault's pin.

## CI

Every target in CI builds the binary and runs `checks/stage-3.sh` to `checks/stage-7.sh` on the
template vault (x64 and ARM64: Windows, macOS, Linux glibc and musl), and every adapter's code path
on fixture installs (`checks/stage-7.sh`). A target counts as verified once that run passes; until
then it is built, not verified.

`badges.yml` redraws the README's live pills daily and on every tag push, and force-pushes them as
the one commit on the orphan `badges` branch; unchanged pills push nothing. Its token can write
contents for that push and nothing else. The runner has no bun, so the workflow fetches one bun
release and checks it against the SHA-256 GitHub records for that asset before it runs; moving bun
means changing `BUN_VERSION` and `BUN_SHA256` together.

## The README's images

Every image in the README is an SVG with its text as outlines, so it renders the same with none of
its fonts installed, in light and dark (`<picture>` follows GitHub's theme). `assets/build.ts` draws
them all, following the CSS of the design previews to the pixel: Chrome's metrics, kerning,
ligatures and wrapping, checked glyph by glyph against the browser.

```bash
bun install --cwd assets
bun --bun assets/build.ts <fonts-dir>
```

`<fonts-dir>` holds static instances of the three variable fonts (Google Fonts, OFL 1.1); the
header of `build.ts` gives the `fonttools varLib.instancer` line for each. The live pills (stars,
the newest tag) cannot be drawn ahead of time: `build.ts` writes `assets/badges/live.json`, the
glyphs and keys they need, and the badges workflow draws them from it with `assets/live.mjs`, with
no fonts and no dependencies.

GitHub takes the social preview and an avatar only as PNG, uploaded by hand (the repo's Settings,
Social preview). `build.ts` writes `social.svg` (1280 x 640) and `avatar.svg` (512 x 512), and any
Chromium browser renders them; with Edge on Windows, from the repo root:

```bash
msedge --headless=new --hide-scrollbars --force-device-scale-factor=1 --window-size=1280,640 --screenshot="$PWD/assets/social.png" "file:///$PWD/assets/social.svg"
msedge --headless=new --hide-scrollbars --force-device-scale-factor=1 --window-size=512,512 --screenshot="$PWD/assets/avatar.png" "file:///$PWD/assets/avatar.svg"
```

### Languages

The README comes in six languages: `README.md` (English) and `i18n/README.<id>.md` for `tr`, `es`,
`pt` (Brazilian), `fr` and `de`, kept out of the root so the file list stays short above the README. Every word drawn into an image lives in `assets/i18n.mjs`, one entry per
language: the hero's rows (`_…_` underlines, `` `…` `` is a code chip), its footer, the pills'
labels and values, and the decimal mark. Names that are commands or features (`prompt hook`,
`guard`, `knowledge find`) stay English in every language.

Each image is written twice over:

| File | Holds | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `<name>-<theme>.svg` | every language, in an SVG `<switch>` | `README.md` |
| `<name>-<id>-<theme>.svg` | that language only | `i18n/README.<id>.md` |

A README cannot see its reader's language, but an image can: in a `<switch>`, the browser draws the
first child whose `systemLanguage` matches any language in its list, by exact tag or by prefix
(`pt` matches `pt-BR`, `pt-BR` does not match `pt`). So English, with no tags, goes last as the
fallback, and a reader with Turkish anywhere in their list sees Turkish even when English comes
first. That is why each translated README names its own fixed files. The all-language file is as
tall as its tallest language, so a shorter one leaves empty space under the hero card.

The fonts are Latin only, so a language in another script needs fonts that cover it first; the
build stops on any letter a font lacks. To add a language: add its entry to `i18n.mjs` (`tags`
lists every regional tag to match, Spanish's `es-419` and `es-MX` among them), write
`i18n/README.<id>.md` with README.md's code blocks and links unchanged (a `../` before each repo
path), add the id to the language row
of every README and to the list in `checks/stage-9.sh`, and run the build. The check fails a
translation whose code blocks, links or images drift from README.md's.

# Benchmark

What the README's numbers are, how each was measured, and how to rerun the ones that can be.

## Tokens to an answer

How much an agent reads to reach the answer to a question: with `knowledge find`, against grep
and the Read tool. **82% fewer tokens overall** on the run below.

| | Found | knowledge | grep + Read | Fewer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Notes, 33 questions | 33/33 | ~80,377 tokens | ~320,211 | **75%** (46% against the best single-word grep) |
| Code, 20 symbols | 20/20 | ~2,866 | ~149,766 | **98%** |
| All | | ~83,242 | ~469,977 | **82%** |

`knowledge find` took ~33.4 ms per question (mean of the per-question medians), `find --code`
~65.5 ms, and `find --code` with `graph --code` ~131.6 ms. Windows 10, Ryzen 5 5500, release
build, 2026-11-24.

### Rerun it

```bash
cargo build --release --locked
bun --bun bench/tokens.ts target/release/knowledge
```

It prints one row per question and the three summary lines above, and removes its temp folder.

### The fixture

The number is public because the fixture is this repository: `template/` as the vault, with
`docs/*.md`, `README.md` (as `Overview.md`) and `AGENTS.md` (as `Agent-Install.md`) added under
`20-Knowledge/knowledge/`; and a clone of its `HEAD` as the checkout. Both sit in a temp folder with
their own `KNOWLEDGE_HOME` and an empty `HOME`, so the binary sees nothing else. The fixture copies
the working tree, so the numbers move a little with the docs; a run is pinned by its commit.

The questions are in [`bench/questions.json`](../bench/questions.json): 33 questions a user asks
about notes, each naming the note that answers it, and 20 symbols, each naming the file that
defines it. The symbols were picked by a rule, not by hand: each `fn` defined once in `src/`, with a
name of 6 or more characters and at least 3 uses across at least 2 files; the first 20 by the SHA-1
of the name.

### The method

Characters are counted, the way the agent's context receives them; tokens are estimated at 4
characters each. The percentages are ratios of characters, so they do not depend on that estimate.

- **knowledge, notes:** `find`'s output, then one whole Read of the note it names. A question whose
  note `find` does not list pays `find`'s output and then grep's whole cost on top.
- **grep, notes, two baselines.** Realistic: grep for every word of the question (stopwords and
  words under 3 letters dropped), rank the files by how many of the words they hold, then by total
  matches, and Read whole files in that order until the answer's note is read. Best case: the one
  word of the question that reaches the note for the least, an oracle no agent has, which only errs
  in grep's favour.
- **knowledge, code:** `find <symbol> --code` and `graph <symbol> --code`, both outputs.
- **grep, code:** `git grep -n -w` over `*.rs *.ts *.mjs *.js *.sh`, then a Read of 40 lines above
  and 5 below each use (where the enclosing function starts), merged per file. The definition's own
  line needs no Read.
- **Reads** are counted as the Read tool returns them: `cat -n` format, a 6-wide line number and a
  tab, at most 2,000 lines.
- **Latency** is the median of 5 runs per question, then the mean across questions, measured from
  process start to exit.

## What it does, by hand

Paths below are Linux; the Windows form follows each block where it differs. `<skeleton>` is the
checkout, `<vault>` the vault, `<dev>` the checkouts folder.

### 1. Prerequisites

`git`, `claude` (Claude Code) and `gitleaks`, all on `PATH`, plus `gh` to check a release's build
provenance, or `cargo` (the Rust toolchain) to build the binary from source instead. The hooks
commit and push their records on their own and scan them with gitleaks first. Without it they
commit nothing.

| Tool | Linux | Windows |
|---|---|---|
| git | your package manager (`pacman -S git`, `apt install git`) | `winget install Git.Git` |
| claude | `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh \| bash` | `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 \| iex` |
| gitleaks | your package manager (`pacman -S gitleaks`, `brew install gitleaks`) | `winget install Gitleaks.Gitleaks` |
| gh | your package manager (`pacman -S github-cli`, `brew install gh`) | `winget install GitHub.cli` |
| cargo | `curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs \| sh` | `winget install Rustlang.Rustup` |

`rust-toolchain.toml` pins the compiler (1.100.0); rustup fetches it on the first build. On Windows
rustup also needs the MSVC build tools (Visual Studio Build Tools, "Desktop development with C++").

`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` must be unset: the hooks read `~/.claude`.

### 2. The vault

A new one from the template, or an existing clone (then skip to `core.fileMode`):

```bash
cp -r <skeleton>/template <vault>
echo '{"version":"0.13.2"}' > <vault>/.skeleton.json     # the version `knowledge --version` prints
git -C <vault> init -b main && git -C <vault> add -A && git -C <vault> commit -m "chore: new vault from knowledge 0.13.2"
git -C <vault> config core.fileMode false
```

`.skeleton.json` pins the skeleton version the vault is written for; each session start compares it
with the checkout. An adopted vault without one is not checked: commit the same file there once.

`core.fileMode false`: Obsidian on Linux rewrites `.obsidian/*.json` with mode 755, and a mode-only
change blocks the SessionStart pull. The vault tracks no executables.

The pre-commit secret scan, in the vault and in the skeleton clone:

```bash
git -C <vault> config core.hooksPath <skeleton>/githooks
git -C <skeleton> config core.hooksPath <skeleton>/githooks
```

`githooks/pre-commit` runs `gitleaks git --staged` on every commit, the hooks' own included, and
refuses the commit when gitleaks is missing. It adds about 1.3 s per commit on Windows.

### 3. config.json

`~/.config/knowledge/config.json` on every OS (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/knowledge/` when set);
`$KNOWLEDGE_CONFIG` overrides it, and `$KNOWLEDGE_HOME` moves the whole folder. On Windows that is
`%USERPROFILE%\.config\knowledge\`, not `%APPDATA%`: a packaged (MSIX) app such as Claude desktop
has its `%APPDATA%` writes redirected to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\<app>\LocalCache\Roaming`, so a
config written from inside it never reaches a plain terminal.

```json
{ "vault": "/home/me/knowledge", "devRoot": "/home/me/dev", "os": "arch",
  "machine": "Free text the SessionStart banner opens with.", "rolloverHour": 5 }
```

`vault` and `devRoot` are required; create `devRoot` if it does not exist. `os` is what logs and
commit notes are stamped with. `rolloverHour` (default 5) is when a daily note starts, local time.
`"pullTrust": "signed"` turns on pull trust; set it last ([security.md](security.md)).

A vault laid out differently names its folders in `folders`; a key left out keeps the default:

```json
{ "folders": { "meta": "Meta", "sessions": "Journal" } }
```

The keys are `meta` (`00-Meta`), `repos` (`10-Repos`), `knowledge` (`20-Knowledge`), `sessions`
(`30-Sessions`), `plans` (`40-Plans`), `ops` (`50-Ops`), `decisions` (`60-Decisions`), `assets`
(`80-Assets`) and `inbox` (`90-Inbox`). A name is one folder at the vault's root: no `/`, `\`, `:`,
`.` or `..`, and no two keys naming one folder. A bad `folders` stops every verb with a line naming
it.

Check what the hooks see (Windows, the home folder shown as `~`):

```
$ knowledge config
{
  "devRoot": "~\\dev",
  "home": "~\\.config\\knowledge",
  "machine": "",
  "os": "windows",
  "pullTrust": "",
  "rolloverHour": 5,
  "skeleton": "~\\dev\\knowledge",
  "source": "~\\.config\\knowledge\\config.json",
  "trustDir": "~\\.config\\knowledge",
  "vault": "~\\knowledge"
}
```

`knowledge config <key>` prints one value, and a folder key prints the name in effect.

### 4. Links into `~/.claude`

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills ~/.agents/skills
for s in <skeleton>/skills/*/; do
  ln -s "${s%/}" ~/.claude/skills/; ln -s "${s%/}" ~/.agents/skills/
done
```

```powershell
foreach ($d in "$HOME\.claude\skills", "$HOME\.agents\skills") {
  New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $d | Out-Null
  Get-ChildItem -Directory C:\dev\knowledge\skills | ForEach-Object {
    New-Item -ItemType Junction -Path "$d\$($_.Name)" -Target $_.FullName } }
```

Every link is a folder's: a junction on Windows, which needs neither Developer Mode nor an
elevated shell. `~/.agents/skills` is the skills folder Codex, opencode, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Amp and
Zed read, so the skills reach them through the same links; opencode reads both folders and loads
each skill once. The `knowledge-*` skills are slash-only (`disable-model-invocation: true`), so
Claude Code keeps their descriptions out of context until you type one. Before 0.13.0 these were
`~/.claude/hooks`, `skills/brain` and `commands/brain-*`, and before 0.13.1 the `knowledge-*` were
`~/.claude/commands/knowledge-*.md` file links: `knowledge setup` removes those links when their
targets end in those paths.

### 5. The knowledge binary

From a release: [§ The binary from a release](#the-binary-from-a-release), into `~/.local/bin`.
From source:

```
$ cargo install --path <skeleton> --locked
$ knowledge --version
knowledge 0.13.2
SQLite 3.54.1, FTS5 on
```

It lands in `~/.cargo/bin` (`%USERPROFILE%\.cargo\bin` on Windows), with `knowledge-code`, the code
map, beside it: `knowledge` hands `find --code`, `graph --code` and `code` to it, and names this
command when it is missing. A clean release build takes two to three minutes; the C compiler SQLite
needs also builds `ring` for `fetch`'s TLS (no CMake, no NASM) and the tree-sitter grammars. Rerun
it after pulling a skeleton whose `src/` changed: the hooks run the installed copy, never the build
folder, and `setup` WARNs when the binary it would register is a build folder's.

Its files live in `~/.config/knowledge` beside `config.json`, unless `KNOWLEDGE_HOME` says
otherwise: `vault-index.db`, `repos-index.db`, `captures.db`, the code maps (`code/<checkout>.db`)
and the hooks' state (`state/`). `fetch` trusts the OS certificate store, so a machine whose store
is out of date fails a TLS handshake rather than falling back to a bundled list.

### 6. The Claude Code plugin

The hooks ship as a plugin, `claude/`, served by this repo's own marketplace
(`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`). Every hook is exec form: the command is
`${user_config.knowledge_bin}` with `["hook", <verb>, "--harness", "claude"]` as its arguments, so
no shell starts per hook and no other `knowledge` earlier on `PATH` can be picked.

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add https://github.com/atlasatakahraman/knowledge
claude plugin install knowledge@knowledge --scope user
```

Then the plugin's one option, in `~/.claude/settings.json`, beside every other key:

```json
{ "pluginConfigs": { "knowledge@knowledge": {
    "options": { "knowledge_bin": "/home/me/.cargo/bin/knowledge" } } } }
```

On Windows the path keeps forward slashes: `"C:/Users/me/.cargo/bin/knowledge.exe"`. Claude Code
reads hooks at session start, so open a new session after.

The marketplace is added with no `autoUpdate`: updates are never automatic ([update.md](update.md)).
`setup` also takes every hook of ours out of `settings.json` that an install before the plugin wrote
(a `knowledge … hook` command, or a `brain-*.mjs` under `~/.claude/hooks`), after the plugin
installs, and keeps every other hook. If the install fails, the apply stops and the old hooks keep
running.

### 7. Identity and Hard-Rules in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`

Both load whole into every session. Add, one import per line:

```markdown
@/home/me/knowledge/00-Meta/Identity.md
@/home/me/knowledge/00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md
```

Never move either behind a link or into a hook: a hook's context is cut to a 2,000-char preview past
10,000 chars. The doctor's `priming` check guards it. `setup` writes the two lines between
`<!-- knowledge-skeleton:begin -->` and `<!-- knowledge-skeleton:end -->`, so `--remove` can take
out exactly that; text outside the markers is never touched. The same generator writes the other
harnesses' blocks (below), and each session start restores a block that went stale.

### 8. The rules lock and the guard

A template vault ships `00-Meta/rules.lock` for its generic packs. For rules you write yourself,
the lock is re-stamped by you, or by your agent once the `rules-files` guard has asked you; a seed
supplies what the text cannot (each rule's kind, enforcement points and the guards):

```bash
cd <vault> && knowledge rules lock --seed <seed.json>   # later edits: knowledge rules lock
knowledge rules check                                   # rules: N units match 00-Meta/rules.lock
```

Commit `00-Meta/rules.lock` with Hard-Rules: the session-start restore takes a changed rule back
from `HEAD` only when `HEAD` matches the lock. The plugin's PreToolUse hook (step 6) is the guard.
Without a lock it allows everything, with one stderr line. `setup` points `core.hooksPath` at
`githooks/` in the vault, this clone and each checkout a `10-Repos` page names. A checkout's own
`core.hooksPath` is kept as `knowledge.ownHooksPath` and runs first. The hook needs `gitleaks` and
`knowledge` on `PATH`, and refuses the commit without either. What the guard can and cannot stop:
[security.md](security.md).

### 9. Compile state

`knowledge compile` turns each finished daily log into notes once, remembered by hash in
`<vault>/50-Ops/brain-compile-state.json` (untracked, per machine). An adopted vault has no state on
a new machine, so the first session would recompile every log it ever had. `setup` marks every log
but today's done: the plan's `compile state` line reads `<file>: N finished log(s) marked
compiled`. This step has no by-hand form: run the plan, even for this line alone. A new vault has
no finished log, so the line reads `ok`.

### 10. First index, and the check

```
$ knowledge doctor --repair --pretty
knowledge doctor  PASS  2026-11-24T10:49:50.767Z
  PASS  vault-index
  PASS  retrieval
  PASS  sessions
  PASS  auth
  PASS  frontmatter
  PASS  links
  PASS  pointers
  PASS  reach
  PASS  ignores
  PASS  commits
  PASS  priming
  PASS  priming-size
  PASS  rules
  PASS  budget
  PASS  skeleton-version
  WARN  hygiene
  WARN  pull-trust
  PASS  codex-trust
  PASS  portable
```

The repair builds the vault index (about a second for 2,000 notes), records commits made outside a
session, regenerates the hub MOCs and brings the index level again. All of it is derived; run it
whenever a check fails. A WARN leaves the doctor at PASS: `hygiene` WARNs while the vault has
uncommitted work, and `pull-trust` until it is set up ([security.md](security.md)). The code map needs no step: each checkout's map is
built by the first `knowledge find <symbol> --code` or `graph <symbol> --code` that names it, and
brought level by every one after.

Then, for a new vault, fill the `<!-- FILL: … -->` placeholders in `00-Meta/Identity.md` and
`00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md` (an agent following [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) asks you about each one), and
replace the questions in `00-Meta/retrieval-cases.json` with ones the vault must always answer.
Then the rules interview: `knowledge rules list` shows the packs, and `knowledge rules enable
<pack>` turns one's guards on; `knowledge rules guard add` gives a rule you write a guard of its own
([verbs.md](verbs.md)). Last, if you want the vault on a second machine, a private repo:
`gh repo create knowledge-vault --private --source <vault> --remote origin --push`.

Each session start runs the full doctor once per logical day, detached, with `--repair --record`;
a FAIL opens the next session with a `!! VAULT HEALTH FAIL` line. No scheduled task is needed.

## Other harnesses

`setup --plan` reaches each of these when its adapter (`adapters/<id>.json`, built into the binary)
detects it, after the Claude part has written `config.json`; `--harness <id>` plans one alone. Each
one's instructions block comes from the same generator as step 7. Codex and opencode cannot import
a file, so their block holds the retrieval steps, then Identity and Hard-Rules written whole. It has
no by-hand form: `setup` writes it, and each session start restores it.

### Codex

Detected by `~/.codex` with `codex` on `PATH`. A Codex plugin has no option to carry an absolute
path, so its hooks run the `knowledge` on `PATH`: `setup` FAILs without one, and WARNs when it is
not the binary that is planning.

```bash
codex plugin marketplace add <skeleton>
codex plugin add knowledge@knowledge
codex mcp add knowledge -- "$(command -v knowledge)" mcp
```

```powershell
codex plugin marketplace add C:\dev\knowledge
codex plugin add knowledge@knowledge
codex mcp add knowledge -- (Get-Command knowledge).Source mcp
```

The block goes into `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` (`%USERPROFILE%\.codex\AGENTS.md`). That global file does
not count toward Codex's 32 KiB `project_doc_max_bytes`, so the cap stays as it is.

- **Hook trust is yours.** Codex runs a plugin hook only after you review it: `/hooks` in the Codex
  CLI. Trust is kept against each hook's hash, so every release asks again. `setup` never writes
  trust: the plan's `hook trust` line and the doctor's `codex-trust` read Codex's own count
  (`codex app-server`, `hooks/list`), and WARN while a hook waits for review. The ChatGPT app's
  Codex runs only hooks already trusted in the CLI and skips the rest without a word.
- **The pin.** Each hook runs `knowledge hook <verb> --harness codex --pin <version>`. A binary of
  another version stands down, and the session start says so in one line. After a new binary,
  `knowledge setup --plan` and `--apply` add the plugin again (a local marketplace has no upgrade
  command); then review the hooks again.
- **The guard denies; it cannot ask.** Codex has no ask, so an ask rule is a deny there and its
  reason says so. An `apply_patch` call is judged by the paths in its patch text.
- **The sandbox.** Codex's elevated Windows sandbox cannot read `~/.config/knowledge`, which also
  holds the signing key, so that folder gets no read grant. Retrieval inside a session goes through
  the `knowledge` MCP server instead: `mcp__knowledge__find` and `mcp__knowledge__graph`, read-only,
  so Codex asks nothing before a call. The block names those tools first.
- **The flush** runs `codex exec --ignore-user-config -m gpt-6-luna -s read-only
  --skip-git-repo-check --json -`, which loads no plugin hook and no MCP server. The global
  `AGENTS.md` still loads: about 30k input tokens a flush.

### opencode

Detected by `~/.config/opencode` with `opencode` on `PATH`. Two files: the plugin, a shim that only
spawns `knowledge hook <verb> --harness opencode` and acts on the reply, and the block in
`~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`. opencode loads every `.ts` in its plugins folder, with no config
entry, in its background service, so restart the service after.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/opencode/plugins && cp <skeleton>/opencode/knowledge.ts ~/.config/opencode/plugins/
opencode service restart
```

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $HOME\.config\opencode\plugins | Out-Null
Copy-Item C:\dev\knowledge\opencode\knowledge.ts $HOME\.config\opencode\plugins\
opencode service restart
```

- `setup` writes the copy built into the binary, pinned to its version, and never overwrites or
  removes a `knowledge.ts` it did not write.
- **The guard** runs in `execute.before` on `shell`, `edit`, `write` and `patch`, and blocks by
  throwing. An ask rule is a deny, as in Codex.
- **The flush** has no transcript file to read: it exports the session (`opencode session export
  --standalone`) and runs `opencode run --standalone -m opencode/tidepool-alpha-free --format json`.
  The model is free, and `--standalone` keeps the flush's marker out of the shared service, where it
  would stand the plugin down in every live session.

### Claude desktop app (Chat)

The Chat has no shell and no hooks, so it gets the vault through `knowledge mcp`: `find`, `graph`
and `read` (one note by name), all read-only, and `note`, which writes and so asks first. Detected by
`~/AppData/Roaming/Claude` or `~/Library/Application Support/Claude`. One key goes into
`claude_desktop_config.json`, every other key kept:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "knowledge": { "command": "/home/me/.cargo/bin/knowledge", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

| Install | The file |
|---|---|
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json` |
| Windows, installer | `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json` |
| Windows, Store (MSIX) | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Claude-Data\<package>\claude_desktop_config.json` |

A Store install leaves only a `.user-data-left.<package>` marker in `%APPDATA%\Claude` and reads the

the plan FAIL rather than replace it. The desktop app's Code tab passes the same server into its
sessions as `mcp__knowledge__*`, so the Claude plugin carries no server of its own.

```bash

knowledge setup --harness generic --instructions <file> --apply <id>
```

# Make a release

For the maintainer. A release is eight archives (`build.yml`'s targets), one `SHA256SUMS` over
them, a build attestation per archive, and `SHA256SUMS.sig`, the maintainer's signature. CI makes
everything but the signature, which is made by hand on the maintainer's machine, so the key never
reaches GitHub. Users check all three: [verify.md](verify.md).

## The release key, once

A key of its own, with a passphrase, kept apart from the per-machine key that signs commits. That
key has no passphrase because the hooks commit with nobody present, so anything running as you
could use it; this one needs you there.

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C knowledge-release -f ~/.ssh/knowledge_release_ed25519
```

Back up the private half offline; it never goes to GitHub or to a second machine. The public half
is the one line of `allowed_signers` at the repo root, limited to file signatures:

```
atlasatakahraman namespaces="file" ssh-ed25519 <the .pub's key> knowledge-release
```

To replace the key, add the new line to `allowed_signers` in a release still signed by the old one,
then drop the old line in the next.

## Each release

1. Set `version` in `Cargo.toml`, run `cargo build` so `Cargo.lock` follows, move every other
   place `git grep` finds the old version (the plugin manifests and pins, the install docs' clone
   tag and archive names), and commit. The workflow refuses a tag that does not name this version.
2. Tag and push the tag. `tag.gpgsign` signs it with the machine key.

   ```bash
   git tag v0.13.2 -m "knowledge 0.13.2: <one line>"
   git push origin v0.13.2
   ```

3. `release.yml` builds the eight archives, writes `SHA256SUMS`, attests each archive and opens a
   **draft** release with them. Nothing is public yet.
4. Sign `SHA256SUMS`, in an empty folder. `ssh-keygen` asks for the passphrase and writes
   `SHA256SUMS.sig`:

   ```bash
   gh release download v0.13.2 -R atlasatakahraman/knowledge -p SHA256SUMS
   ssh-keygen -Y sign -f ~/.ssh/knowledge_release_ed25519 -n file SHA256SUMS
   ```

5. Check the signature with [verify.md](verify.md) step 1 against the repo's `allowed_signers`,
   then attach it:

   ```bash
   gh release upload v0.13.2 SHA256SUMS.sig -R atlasatakahraman/knowledge
   ```

6. Download one archive from the draft and run all of [verify.md](verify.md) on it. Then publish:

   ```bash
   gh release edit v0.13.2 --draft=false -R atlasatakahraman/knowledge
   ```

`workflow_dispatch` on `release.yml` is the dry run: the archives and `SHA256SUMS` are left as the
run's artifacts, with no attestation and no release.

# Security

What the engine protects, how, and what it cannot stop. To report a vulnerability:
[SECURITY.md](../.github/SECURITY.md).

## What it touches

- **Writes:** the vault, `~/.config/knowledge` (the config, the indexes, the hooks' state, an
  optional signing key), and the files `setup` lists in its plan before it writes them
  ([install.md](install.md)). `setup --remove` takes out everything but the data
  ([remove.md](remove.md)).
- **Network:** `git pull` and the records push to your vault's own remote; `fetch`, when you or the
  agent run it; `update --plan`, when you run it; the headless flush and compile, through the
  harness's own CLI and account. No hook phones a server of ours, and nothing checks for updates on
  its own.
- **Never read:** harness credentials (`~/.claude/.credentials.json`, `~/.codex/auth.json`). The
  engine runs the harness's CLI and lets it sign in itself.

## Credential fences

Recommended for `~/.claude/settings.json`; `setup` never writes it, since security settings stay
yours:

```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Read(~/.ssh/**)",
      "Read(~/.codex/auth.json)",
      "Read(~/.claude/.credentials.json)",
      "Read(**/.env*)",
      "Read(~/.config/knowledge/signing_ed25519)"
    ]
  }
}
```

Merge it into an existing `permissions.deny`. These rules cover the Read tool; a shell command can
still read the files, so keep shell commands on approval. Codex's elevated Windows sandbox cannot
read `~/.config/knowledge`, and that folder gets no read grant, since it holds the signing key:
retrieval inside Codex goes through the read-only `knowledge` MCP server instead.

## Signing and pull trust

Commits from every machine are signed with an SSH key, and each session start pulls only a tip
signed by a key you listed. The key has no passphrase, because the hooks commit with nobody present;
it signs commits and tags, and nothing else. A release is signed by a separate key with a
passphrase, so a process running as you can't sign one ([release.md](release.md)); this repo's own
`allowed_signers` holds that key, and the per-machine one below holds the commit keys. In this
order, because step 4 is the one that can refuse a pull:

1. **Each machine:** `knowledge setup --plan --signing`, then `--apply` its id. It writes
   `~/.config/knowledge/signing_ed25519`, sets `gpg.format ssh`, `user.signingkey`,
   `commit.gpgsign` and `tag.gpgsign` in the vault and in the skeleton clone, and adds this
   machine's key to `~/.config/knowledge/allowed_signers`.
   `ssh-keygen -lf ~/.config/knowledge/signing_ed25519.pub` prints its fingerprint. Add the public
   key on GitHub as a **signing** key (`gh ssh-key add <key>.pub --type signing`; needs
   `gh auth refresh -s admin:ssh_signing_key`).
2. **Each machine:** add the other machine's public key to `allowed_signers`, one line each:
   `<email> namespaces="git" ssh-ed25519 AAAA…`. Fetch it from
   `https://api.github.com/users/<you>/ssh_signing_keys`, and compare its fingerprint
   (`ssh-keygen -lf <file>`) with the one the other machine printed before trusting it.
3. **Both machines at the same tip** of the vault and the skeleton, so the first checked pull is a
   signed commit.
4. **Each machine:** `"pullTrust": "signed"` in `config.json`. Then, on GitHub, a ruleset that
   requires signed commits on `main`, once every machine signs.

Only the tip of a pull is checked: a signed tip vouches for the unsigned commits under it. `%G?`
must be `G`; `U` (a good signature from a key not in `allowed_signers`) is refused, and so is a
missing `allowed_signers`. `allowed_signers` is passed on each call, never read from the repo's
config. The doctor's `pull-trust` check WARNs until step 4 and FAILs if a piece goes missing.
Undo, at any step: `git config --unset commit.gpgsign` in a clone, or remove `pullTrust`.

## Rules and the guard

`00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md` stays one note, loaded whole. Each `##` section is a pack, and each rule is
a bullet that opens with a bold line, whose slug is the rule's id. `00-Meta/rules.lock` holds what
the text cannot: each rule's kind, enforcement points and hash, and the guards.

- **The guard** (`hook pre-tool`, on each harness's pre-tool event for shell, edit and MCP calls)
  splits a shell line into segments and words, and answers `deny` or `ask` with the rule's id. It
  reads only `rules.lock`. It prints nothing when it allows, and on a missing or broken lock it
  allows with one stderr line. Codex and opencode cannot ask, so an ask rule is a deny there.
- **The backstop** is `githooks/pre-commit`. It runs the repo's own hook, gitleaks, then
  `rules check --staged`, which fails a commit holding a guard's staged names or a Hard-Rules that
  disagrees with the lock.
- **The restore.** Each session start runs `rules check --restore`. A rule that differs from the
  lock comes back from `HEAD` when `HEAD` matches the lock, and one line says so. Otherwise the
  doctor FAILs until you relock or revert.

**What it cannot stop.** An agent that runs code as you can change any file you can. The guard puts
the plain forms to you: an Edit, `sed -i`, a redirect, `Set-Content`. It cannot judge a wrapper (an
interpreter's `-e`, a command substitution, an escape). That case is caught afterwards, by the next
session start's restore and the doctor. A harness with no hooks (the `generic` adapter, the desktop
Chat) gets the rules as text only; the pre-commit backstop still runs in every clone `setup` set.

## What `fetch` refuses

Before it connects: anything but `http` and `https`, credentials in a URL, and any host that
resolves to a loopback, private (RFC 1918), link-local, unique-local, CGNAT, multicast or
unspecified address, IPv4 inside IPv6 included. It connects only to the addresses it checked,
follows at most 5 redirects and checks each one again, stops at 20 s and 5 MB, reads no proxy from
the environment, and stores only HTML (converted), other text and JSON. `--allow-private` lifts the
address check and nothing else. TLS uses the OS certificate store, with no bundled root list.

## Secrets in commits

Every commit in the vault, the skeleton clone and each checkout `setup` set runs `gitleaks git
--staged` first, and the records push runs gitleaks before it commits. Without gitleaks on `PATH`,
the hook refuses the commit and the records stay uncommitted.

# Troubleshooting

Start with `knowledge doctor --pretty`: each FAIL names what it found. `knowledge doctor --repair`
rebuilds everything derived (the index, the hubs, the commit notes) and is safe to run any time.

| Symptom | Cause, and the fix |
|---|---|
| `link FAIL ... Developer Mode` on Windows | A file symlink needs Developer Mode (Settings > For developers) or an elevated shell |
| `setup: the plan changed since --plan` | A target changed after the plan was printed, or the flags differ: plan again and read it |
| A plan line `FAIL` | It names what to fix; a plan with a FAIL has no id to apply |
| `ignores` FAIL on a fresh clone | `.obsidian/app.json`'s `userIgnoreFilters` names a folder git did not bring: an empty folder needs a `.gitkeep` |
| `links` FAIL on a fresh clone, pointing at a date | A record links a daily log that was never committed: commit it, or let the flush write it |
| `vault-index` FAIL, `stale:` or `missing:` | A note changed outside a session and outside the hooks: `knowledge doctor --repair` |
| `!! SKELETON x is behind the vault's pin y` at session start | The other machine moved the vault to a newer skeleton: `git -C <skeleton> pull --ff-only`, then rebuild ([update.md](update.md)) |
| `!! SKELETON x is ahead of the vault's pin y` | The skeleton moved on: read its changes since `y` (`git -C <skeleton> log vy..`), adapt the vault, set `.skeleton.json` to `x`, commit |
| `!! VAULT PULL refused: the tip is not signed by a known key` | Pull trust is on and origin's tip is unsigned or signed by a key not in `allowed_signers`: check who pushed it (`git log --show-signature -1 @{u}`) before adding a key ([security.md](security.md)) |
| `!! VAULT PULL skipped: incoming commits touch files with uncommitted changes` | Origin changed files you also changed and have not committed; git merged nothing. Commit or stash those files, then `git pull --ff-only`. Uncommitted changes elsewhere never block the pull |
| `pre-commit: gitleaks is not on PATH; commit refused` | Install gitleaks ([install.md](install.md)), or the commit stays unscanned |
| `pin FAIL` in the plan | The adopted vault pins another version: check out that one, or adapt the vault and bump the pin |
| Every hook errors with `no knowledge config` | `config.json` is missing, or `$KNOWLEDGE_CONFIG` points somewhere empty ([install.md](install.md)) |
| Every verb stops with a line naming `folders` | `config.json`'s `folders` holds a bad name: one folder per key, no `/`, `\`, `:`, `.` or `..` |
| A commit fails in a hook right after a skeleton pull | The hook calls a verb the installed binary does not have yet: rebuild it ([update.md](update.md)) |
| `this binary is x, but the codex plugin's hooks were written for y, so they stand down` | A new binary and an old plugin: `knowledge setup --plan`, `--apply`, then the Codex hook review |
| `WARN hook trust 0 of 9 hooks trusted in Codex` | The hooks wait for your review: `/hooks` in the Codex CLI |
| `knowledge find` in Codex: `Access denied (os error 5)` on `config.json` | Codex's Windows sandbox: the model should use `mcp__knowledge__find`; `codex mcp list` must show `knowledge` |
| `cargo install` on Windows cannot replace `knowledge.exe` (access denied) | A running `knowledge mcp` holds the file: the Claude desktop app's server, or Codex's or opencode's. Quit the app fully (the tray too), install, start it again; a session inside that app stops with it, its background tasks included |
| opencode runs none of the hooks after setup | The service loaded its plugins before the file existed: `opencode service restart` |
| The desktop Chat lists no `knowledge` tools | The config is in a folder the app left (a Store install reads `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Claude-Data\<package>`), or the app was not fully restarted |
| `auth` FAIL, or the flush times out after 120 s | The harness's CLI is signed out, and a signed-out CLI waits: sign in to it in a terminal (`claude`, then `/login`) |

# Update

Nothing updates on its own. No hook, session start or background task checks for a new version:
an updater that phones home is a telemetry surface, so the check runs only when you ask for it.

## Ask what is new

```
$ knowledge update --plan
knowledge 0.13.2, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
latest release: v0.13.2  https://github.com/atlasatakahraman/knowledge/releases/tag/v0.13.2
This binary is the latest release. Nothing to do.
```

Before the first release it named the checkout's steps instead (`pull --ff-only`, `cargo install`,
then the plan).

It makes one HTTPS call, to GitHub's API for the latest release, and sends nothing about you or
your vault. Once a release exists, it names it and prints this platform's steps: the archive,
`SHA256SUMS` and `SHA256SUMS.sig` to download, [verify.md](verify.md)'s three checks, the folder to
extract the two binaries into, the checkout's move to the new tag (a checkout installed from a
release sits on its tag, and its plugins must carry the binary's version or the hooks stand down),
and the plan to run after. It downloads nothing and replaces nothing. 0.13.0 prints no checkout
step; from it, run `git -C <checkout> fetch --tags` and `git -C <checkout> checkout v<new>` before
the plan.
The release key it prints is the one built into your binary, so the new release is checked against
a key you already trust rather than one fetched beside the archive.
`--apply` is not built: on Windows a running `knowledge mcp` (the Claude desktop app, Codex,
opencode) holds the binary, so the replace is a step you take with those apps quit.

## From the checkout

The skeleton checkout fast-forwards itself at each session start, unless origin changed a file you
have uncommitted changes in. After a
pull that changed `src/`, rebuild the binary, then plan:

```bash
cargo install --path <skeleton> --locked
knowledge setup --plan
knowledge setup --apply <id>
```

The hooks run the installed binary, never the build folder, so until the rebuild they run the old
one. The plan moves the Codex and opencode plugins to the new version's pin, and Codex asks for its
hook review again (`/hooks` in the Codex CLI).

## The Claude Code plugin

The marketplace is added with no `autoUpdate`. Once that flag is set, Claude Code copies it into
`~/.claude/plugins/known_marketplaces.json`, where it stays even after it is removed from
`settings.json`. The plugin's version is the binary's, and Claude Code replaces a cached plugin
only when that version changes. It compares against its own clone of the marketplace, which
nothing refreshes on its own, so `claude plugin update` alone reports the old version as the
latest. When a pull changes `claude/`, the session start names the three steps:

```bash
claude plugin marketplace update knowledge
claude plugin update knowledge@knowledge
```

then `/reload-plugins` in a running session.

## The vault's pin

When the skeleton's version moves past the vault's `.skeleton.json`, the session start says which
side moves. Read what changed since the pin (`git -C <skeleton> log v<pin>..`), adapt the vault,
set `.skeleton.json` to the new version, and commit it.

## From before 0.12.0

The code map replaced graphify in 0.12.0. On a machine set up before it, the next plan removes the
graphify server `setup` registered, in Claude Code and in Codex, and leaves a graphify server of
your own as it is. graphify itself is yours to uninstall: `uv tool uninstall graphifyy`.

How each step was first done: [install.md](install.md). When a step fails:
[troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md).
