# Verify a release

Check an archive before you extract it. Three checks, each answering a different question:

| Check | Answers | Trusts |
|---|---|---|
| The signature over `SHA256SUMS` | Did the maintainer approve exactly these bytes? | Only the release key, which never leaves the maintainer's machine |
| The checksum | Is your archive the one `SHA256SUMS` lists? | The signed `SHA256SUMS` |
| The build provenance | Was the archive built by this repository's release workflow, from the tag? | GitHub and the workflow |

The signature is the one that does not trust GitHub: anyone who could rewrite a release (a stolen
token, a compromised build step) could replace the archives and `SHA256SUMS` together, but not
sign them. Run the signature first, then the checksum; the provenance adds GitHub's word on how the
bytes were built.

All three OSes ship OpenSSH with `ssh-keygen -Y verify` (OpenSSH 8.2 or later; Windows 10 and 11
have it in `C:\Windows\System32\OpenSSH`). The provenance needs the GitHub CLI, `gh`.

## Download

From the release page, into an empty folder: your platform's archive, `SHA256SUMS` and
`SHA256SUMS.sig`. Then `allowed_signers` from the same tag:

```
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/atlasatakahraman/knowledge/v0.13.2/allowed_signers
```

It holds one line, the release key:

```
atlasatakahraman namespaces="file" ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIOQM0nPqBftl8DiBjK/iwZNA0Ut7iamaOJhVMXJk1Dy7 knowledge-release
```

Its fingerprint is `SHA256:4lk0qVkGnFfrnKNselpgVf9e55AvCRSy5OkdhcCq6uc`. A copy fetched from the same place as the archive proves
only as much as that place, so compare the fingerprint with one you got elsewhere: the copy in the
checkout or binary you already trust (`knowledge update --plan` prints the line it was built with),
or this page at an older tag.

## 1. The signature

```bash
ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I atlasatakahraman -n file -s SHA256SUMS.sig < SHA256SUMS
```

```powershell
cmd /c "ssh-keygen -Y verify -f allowed_signers -I atlasatakahraman -n file -s SHA256SUMS.sig < SHA256SUMS"
```

PowerShell has no `<`, and piping the file through it would change its bytes, so `cmd` reads it.
A good signature prints the key's fingerprint and exits 0:

```
Good "file" signature for atlasatakahraman with ED25519 key SHA256:4lk0qVkGnFfrnKNselpgVf9e55AvCRSy5OkdhcCq6uc
```

A changed `SHA256SUMS` exits non-zero:

```
Could not verify signature.
Signature verification failed: incorrect signature
```

So does a signature made for anything but a file (`-n file`), such as a commit:

```
Could not verify signature.
Couldn't verify signature: namespace does not match
```

## 2. The checksum

```bash
grep -F "  knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz" SHA256SUMS | sha256sum -c -
```

```
knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz: OK
```

On macOS, `shasum -a 256 -c -` in place of `sha256sum -c -`. On Windows:

```powershell
$f = "knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip"
((Get-FileHash $f -Algorithm SHA256).Hash + "  $f") -in (Get-Content SHA256SUMS)
```

`True` is a match. `False` is a changed archive, or a name that is not in `SHA256SUMS`.

## 3. The build provenance

```bash
gh attestation verify knowledge-0.13.2-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz \
  --repo atlasatakahraman/knowledge \
  --signer-workflow atlasatakahraman/knowledge/.github/workflows/release.yml \
  --source-ref refs/tags/v0.13.2 --deny-self-hosted-runners
```

It checks the archive's attestation in Sigstore's public transparency log: built by `release.yml`,
from the tag, on a GitHub-hosted runner. It exits 0 on a match. An archive with no attestation
exits 1:

```
Error: HTTP 404: Not Found (https://api.github.com/repos/atlasatakahraman/knowledge/attestations/sha256:…)
```

## Then

Extract, put `knowledge` and `knowledge-code` on your `PATH` side by side, and follow
[install.md](install.md) from `knowledge setup --plan`, or [update.md](update.md) over an older
version. How a release is made and signed: [release.md](release.md).

# Conventions

The vault schema. The hooks, the `/knowledge` skill and `knowledge doctor` all assume it.

## Frontmatter

Every note. `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` and `LICENSE*` are the only exemptions.

```yaml
---
type: identity|rules|moc|repo|architecture|decision|session|plan|doc|usage|commit|commits|task|person
project: <the repo's remote name in lowercase> | knowledge
tags: [topic, topic]
created: 2026-01-01
updated: 2026-01-02
status: active | draft | superseded | in-progress | complete | done | legacy
---
```

`type` and `created` are required: the doctor's `frontmatter` check and the post-edit
hook's write-time check fail without them. `project` is required for anything repo-scoped; the vault itself
is `knowledge`. `updated` changes on every edit. A `status: superseded` note keeps a link to what
replaced it.

`commit` is one per-commit note, written by the commit recorder (`knowledge hook post-bash`); `commits` is its generated month index.
`moc` is a map of content, hand-written or generated by `knowledge hubs`.

## Naming

- **Files:** kebab-case. `retry-backoff.md`, not `Retry Backoff.md`. A repo's folder note takes its
  remote's exact casing (`My-App.md`).
- **MOCs:** `00-MOC-<Scope>.md`, one per folder. Always sorts first.
- **Every basename is unique across the vault.** Obsidian and `knowledge` resolve `[[name]]` by
  filename, so two notes with one name make every link to either ambiguous. That is why there is no
  `about.md`, `plan.md` or `index.md` anywhere.
- **Folder notes:** a folder's main note is `<Folder>/<Folder>.md` (`10-Repos/My-App/My-App.md`,
  `40-Plans/<slug>/<slug>.md`). Other notes in the folder get specific names, never generic ones.
- **Repo names are the GitHub remote's exact casing**, in `10-Repos/`, `60-Decisions/Repos/` and
  `80-Assets/Repos/` alike. One name, three places, no aliases.
- **Plans:** every plan lives in the vault, one-repo plans included. One folder each:
  `40-Plans/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>/` holding `<slug>.md` (diagnosis + stages), and optionally
  `<slug>-spec.md`, `<slug>-implementation.md`, `stages/`, `evidence/`.
- **Decisions (ADRs):** `60-Decisions/Repos/<Remote-Name>/<NNNN>-<slug>.md` for one repo;
  `60-Decisions/Identity/<NNNN>-<slug>.md` for the vault, its hooks, or how the agent behaves.
  `<NNNN>` is a per-folder sequence from `0001`. Never inside a checkout.
- **Records** (daily notes, commit notes) are reached through a generated index (`00-MOC-Sessions`,
  `commits-YYYY-MM`) that is itself at most 2 hops from the root MOC. Never edit a generated index by
  hand; `knowledge hubs` and the commit recorder rewrite them.
- **Generated month files** share one scheme: `commits-YYYY-MM`, `usage-YYYY-MM-<os>` (one per boot), `health-YYYY-MM`.

## Links

**Wikilinks for every cross-reference:** `[[note-name]]`. Obsidian and `knowledge graph` both traverse them;
a markdown path link is invisible to the graph.

Link liberally. A `[[link]]` to a note that doesn't exist yet is not an error, it marks something
worth writing, **provided it is listed in [[Forward-Links]]**. An unlisted unresolved link is a bug,
and `knowledge doctor` reports it.

**Never path-qualify a link** (`[[00-Meta/Conventions]]`): it breaks on every move. Basenames are
unique, so a plain `[[Conventions]]` always resolves. Link syntax quoted in prose, or in a commit
body (which the commit recorder copies into the vault verbatim), goes in backticks.

## Reach

Every note is at most **2 hops** from [[00-MOC-Root]]; a record at most 3. the doctor's
`reach` check enforces it. A new note goes into its folder's MOC when it is written:
`knowledge compile` does this for the notes it creates, under an `Unsorted (brain-compile)` heading.

## Note shape

**One concept per note.** If a note needs two MOC entries, it is two notes.

A repository's page in `10-Repos/` is an index entry, not documentation: what the repo is, its
licence, its `checkout:` pointer, and a **"Known gaps — don't chase these"** section. That section
stops an agent re-investigating something already decided.

`checkout: <Remote-Name>` and `docs: <Remote-Name>/docs` are relative to `devRoot` in
`config.json`, so one note resolves on every machine. the doctor's `pointers` check fails on an absolute pointer
and on one into a cloned checkout that does not exist; a repo this machine never cloned is listed,
not failed.

## Where things live

| Content | Location |
|---|---|
| Repo-specific docs | the repo's own `docs/`: it **is** the repo's wiki page |
| Plans, all of them | `40-Plans/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>/`: [[00-MOC-Plans]] |
| Reusable knowledge | `20-Knowledge/<Category>/`: [[00-MOC-Knowledge]] |
| People the owner knows | `20-Knowledge/People/<first-last>/<first-last>.md`, `type: person`, one folder each: [[00-MOC-People]] |
| Daily logs | `30-Sessions/YYYY/MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`, split at the configured rollover hour |
| Decisions | `60-Decisions/Repos/<Remote-Name>/` · `60-Decisions/Identity/`: [[00-MOC-Decisions]] |
| Commit and usage records | `50-Ops/Commits/<YYYY-MM>/` + `commits-YYYY-MM.md` · `50-Ops/Usage/usage-YYYY-MM-<os>.md`: [[00-MOC-Ops]] |
| Attachments | `80-Assets/Images/` · `80-Assets/Diagrams/`: Obsidian's `attachmentFolderPath` |
| Repo brand assets | `80-Assets/Repos/<Remote-Name>/`: masters; the export ships in the repo |
| Unsorted | `90-Inbox/`: empty it, don't let it become an archive |

**Nothing is duplicated between the vault and a repo.** A repo's docs stay in the repo; the vault
links to them.

## Renaming a repository

Path-based ignores go stale on a rename, silently: Obsidian's `userIgnoreFilters` just stops
matching (the doctor's `ignores` check names a stale one). After renaming a repo:

1. Rename its `10-Repos/<Remote-Name>/` folder and folder note, and `60-Decisions/Repos/<Remote-Name>/`,
   to the remote's exact casing; update the `checkout:` pointer (the doctor's `pointers` check fails on a dead one).
2. The code map is kept per checkout folder (`code/<Remote-Name>.db` in the knowledge home): the
   first `knowledge find <symbol> --code` under the new name builds its map. Delete the old name's
   file.

On a case-insensitive filesystem a stale lowercase path resolves to the renamed folder and appears
to work. A wrong-but-working link is worse than a broken one.

# Hard Rules

Non-negotiable. These apply in every session without being restated: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
imports this note whole. Who I am: [[Identity]]. Each `##` section is a pack and each bullet's
bold line is a rule; `rules.lock` beside this note holds their kinds, enforcement points and
hashes. `knowledge rules list` shows the packs, and `knowledge rules enable|disable <pack>` turns
one on or off. Every `FILL:` comment marks a placeholder.

## Tooling

Knowledge work goes through `knowledge`: it costs fewer tokens and reaches more.

<!-- FILL: package manager, runtimes, and which tool to prefer over which in your stack. -->

- **If `knowledge` has an equivalent, use it.**

| Instead of | Use | When |
|---|---|---|
| Bash + Read | `<cmd> \| knowledge keep "<label>" --q "<q>"` | Output over ~2,000 chars to filter or search. `keep` prints 2,000 chars at most, so anything shorter is cheaper read whole |
| WebFetch | `knowledge fetch <url> --q "<q>"` | Any web page: Markdown back, private addresses refused |
| Re-reading a vault note | `knowledge find "<q>"`, from any folder | It's in the vault index |
| Re-reading a repo doc, or a kept/fetched output | `knowledge find "<q>" --repo [<name>]` / `--captures` | It's indexed (captures: 14 days) |
| Reading notes to see how they connect | `knowledge graph <note> [<note>]` | A note's links in and out, or the path between two |
| Grep or Read across a checkout for a symbol | `knowledge find <symbol> --code` / `knowledge graph <symbol> [<symbol>] --code` | Where it is defined, what uses it and what it uses, or the path between two |
| — | `WebSearch`, used **directly** | Finding URLs: titles + URLs + a short synthesis, not pages |

**Web pattern:** `WebSearch` to find → `knowledge fetch` to read → `knowledge find --captures` to
re-query. Nothing blocks `WebFetch`: this rule is what keeps it out.

- **No default tool without a reason that can be named.** `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Bash` and
  `WebFetch` are the exception: the exact bytes for an `Edit`, a file under the ~4 KB break-even
  that a retrieval tier already named, an image, short fixed output, or mutating state.
  Convenience is not a reason. Recon is `knowledge find --code` / `graph --code` for the code and
  `knowledge keep` / `find` for the reads.
- **All file writes use native `Write` / `Edit`.** Before an `Edit` or `Write` of an existing file,
  read it with the native `Read` tool in this session, the lines to change (offset and limit) at
  least. A `cat`, `sed -n` or `grep` through a shell does not count.
- **The repos' code goes through the code map.** `knowledge find <symbol> --code` says where a
  symbol is defined, `knowledge graph <symbol> [<other>] --code` what uses it and how two connect:
  one SQLite file per checkout, brought level before every answer, zero tokens.
- **Retrieval health, zero tokens:** `knowledge doctor --pretty` asserts the vault index is
  complete and the questions in `retrieval-cases.json` return the right note.

## Code

- **The least code that solves the problem.** Before writing, in order: does it need to exist;
  does this codebase already have it (a helper, type or pattern a few files over); does the
  standard library, then the platform (`<input type="date">`, CSS, a DB constraint), then an
  installed dependency cover it; only then the minimum code. No abstraction for a need that has
  not arrived: no interface with one implementation, no config for a value that never changes, no
  scaffolding for later. Fewest files, shortest diff, boring over clever. Of two equal options,
  the one correct on edge cases.
- **Read the problem fully before choosing the smallest change.** Trace the real flow end to end
  first; the smallest change in the wrong place is a second bug. Research first, never edit first:
  plan the steps (which files to read, in what order, with which tools), read the actual code, docs
  or output, and reason from that, never from an assumption; then make the smallest surgical edit,
  never a whole-file rewrite or a sweeping change.
- **Fix the cause, at the place every caller passes through.** A report names a symptom: find
  every caller of the function before editing, and one guard in the shared function beats one per
  caller. A problem met while working is owned, not labelled: "not caused by my changes",
  "pre-existing", "known limitation" and "future work" are never a reason to leave it. Find its
  cause and fix it; only I defer. **Narrow boundaries before forming a hypothesis:** instrument
  each layer (call it directly, check whether state exists) before proposing fixes, and
  reconstruct what actually ran rather than what should have. Three failures on the same fix →
  question the architecture, not just the latest symptom.
- **Never simplify away** input validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data
  loss, security measures, accessibility basics, or anything explicitly requested.
- **No refactor of code the task didn't name.** No drive-by cleanups, no renames, no reformatting
  adjacent code. The exception is dead code that is the actual cause of a bug: cleaning it up is
  part of the fix.
- **Features land in dependency order, not speculatively.** Nothing is wired ahead of the thing
  that would trigger it.
- **Code a person reads in one pass, with a comment that says why.** A mechanical fix carries the
  why, not just the value, so the next reader does not "correct" it back. A deliberate
  simplification with a known ceiling (a global lock, an O(n²) scan) gets a comment naming the
  ceiling and the upgrade path.
- **Self-review of a commit covers logic, duplication, and speed, efficiency and security.**
  Self-checks run in loops while working, not once at the end: before a commit or a question to
  me, re-read the diff against the request, re-run the check, and fix what it finds first.

## Git

- **Nothing is committed until I give an explicit go, and each push needs its own yes.** While I
  am still deciding how something should work, leave changes uncommitted. Run `git log` first,
  because the nightly compile may already have committed the files. Before a push, run
  `git fetch` and `git log origin/main..main`: a push sends every unpushed commit. Ask, then wait.
- **Commit by area, each commit building on its own, the vault in its own commit.** Never a
  non-compiling intermediate commit. Every commit has a body that says why: the vault records the
  body as the commit's reason, so a subject-only commit leaves an empty record. Stage only the
  named paths, never a whole folder.
- **Gate before every commit: types, lint, build, secret scan — all four, every time.** Errors
  already there are fixed too, in their own commit, so the change's diff stays its own; new ones
  from the change block it.
- **Session records are committed through `knowledge records`,** which runs the secret scan,
  never by hand.

## Questions and reports

- **Questions go through the harness's question tool, never as plain text in a message.** In
  Claude Code that is AskUserQuestion: interviews, brainstorms, approvals, every choice, up to four
  per call, recommendation first. When the tool is missing, say which one and why before falling
  back.
- **Never skip the interview, the brainstorm or the questions.** Creative work and anything built
  on a reference I named start with questions: recon first, then the questions, then the work. A
  name that resolves to one match is not an answer; when a reference could mean more than one
  thing, ask which before building.
- **Ask open questions immediately, once, with a concrete reading.** If there's a confident
  recommendation, give it and move on rather than parking the question. When an answer of mine can
  be read two ways, ask one question that states the reading, then build on the confirmed one.
- **Nothing stays "open" without my say-so, every time.** A report never ends with an "Open" or
  "Found, not fixed" list that I didn't approve. For each item that would stay open, ask me first
  (fix now / defer to a named stage or task / drop), with a recommendation, and act on the answer.
  Deferring one item does not approve deferring the next.
- **Ask before a fix that would reverse an earlier decision** — a fix that undoes a prior choice
  gets a question first, not a silent flip.

## Verification

- **Verification tasks are comprehensive by default**, not spot checks: "verify X" means the whole
  set against the live thing, not a sample.
- **Clean startup matters** — no plugin or tool loading errors. Catch duplicate keymaps or
  malformed specs early rather than letting them surface as runtime noise.
- **Before marking UI work done, click through every interaction in a real browser and read the
  console** — not just the golden path, and runtime, hydration and CSP errors, not just visual
  layout.
- **Verify across every context before marking complete** — a control gets checked on every ground
  it can land on and in every state (resting, hover, focus), with the worst case written down.
- **Idle machine for latency timing.** CPU-heavy work (builds, lint) waits until a timing run
  finishes.
- **Comparing configs across platforms — check file counts and sizes first** to scope the diff,
  before reading files.

## Safety

- **Never push to production/deploy autonomously** — explicit "yes" first, every time, even
  mid-task. Reuse an already-running dev server instead of killing and restarting it.
- **Read-only `SELECT`s on production are allowed when I ask, for diagnosis.** Writes and log pulls
  still need a yes. A check that needs a production setting changed is reported unverified, not
  passed.
- **Security config is applied before it is committed and pushed, not after.**
- **A perf optimization that requires disabling a security control** — measure the actual savings
  first. If the gain is under ~5% of total cost, keep the control enabled.
- **Deletions are measured and shown, and nothing goes until I pick.** Measure read-only first,
  present a table, delete nothing until I pick, and check that no process holds a folder. Before
  deleting scratch files, confirm a durable note holds what they recorded.
- **Inspecting sensitive system files (disk images, guest disks) — read-only mounts and copies
  only.** Never attach or write to the original.
- **Privileged probes auto-revert.** Temporary firewall rules, kernel settings and similar tweaks
  made to test something are removed on exit, and a failed retest rolls back on its own.
- **Don't spend paid credits on a test run without asking first.** Cost quotes and model listings
  are free to check; a real submit waits for my yes.

## Knowledge

- **Never move primed content behind a link.** Identity and Hard-Rules load whole every session;
  splitting either into linked notes means the part behind the link is missed whenever the link is
  not followed. Grow the note; do not split it.
- **One-way or hard-to-reverse decisions get a standing note in `CLAUDE.md`.** Not just recorded
  in a decision note: a note in the repo instructions catches a future re-proposal before it gets
  re-litigated.
- **Write notes through `/knowledge new <kind>` and `/knowledge edit <kind>`.** They know the schema in
  [[Conventions]] and keep every note reachable from [[00-MOC-Root]].
- **Retrieval runs in tiers, in order** ([[Retrieval-Protocol]]). Never sweep the vault with `ls`,
  `find` or `grep`: the MOC answers "where is X" in one hop.

# Hook lifecycle

Every hook that touches this vault: its event, what it does, what it writes, what it costs, and
what notices when it breaks. The rationale is in [[Why-This-Exists]].

Every hook is the `knowledge` binary's `hook` verb, and reads its paths from the machine's
`config.json`. Claude Code gets the hooks from the skeleton's plugin, `knowledge@knowledge`,
which `knowledge setup` installs: each hook is exec form, `${user_config.knowledge_bin}` with
`["hook", <verb>, "--harness", "claude"]`, so no shell starts and no other `knowledge` on PATH is
picked. Other harnesses run the same verbs (§ Other harnesses). What a hook starts in the background
is the same binary again, detached, so no hook starts a JavaScript runtime. The watermarks, locks
and exports live in `state/` beside the config (`~/.config/knowledge/state`, or `$KNOWLEDGE_HOME/state`);
the first run moves an older `~/.claude/hooks/.state` there. The `/knowledge` skill and the
slash-only `knowledge-*` skills link into the checkout, and the doctor's `skeleton-version` check fails when they do not.
`.skeleton.json` at the vault root pins the skeleton version the vault is written for: the session
start says so when the checkout is another version, and `skeleton-version` fails.

Every hook **fails silent at runtime**: it exits 0 and never blocks the session. The last column
says what notices a failure.

## Registered hooks

Runs `knowledge rules check --restore`. Then injects what changes per session: the current OS, the retrieval order, the flush canary, any recorded `claude -p` failure, the health alarm, and how many captured decisions wait for promotion. Identity and Hard-Rules are **not** injected here: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` imports both whole, because a hook's context past 10,000 chars is cut to a preview. Prints nothing when it allows | — | ~20 ms | the doctor's `rules`; the pre-commit backstop |

detached child carries `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY`, and every hook verb exits at once when it is set, so a
flush's own `claude -p` cannot re-fire capture.

## Other harnesses

Each harness is an adapter (`adapters/<id>.json`, built into the binary) that maps its own event
names onto the same verbs, plus a translator that reads its payload and words the reply. The rows
above hold for each; what differs is below. Setup and the by-hand steps: the skeleton's
`docs/install.md` § Other harnesses.

| Codex CLI | The Codex plugin `knowledge@knowledge`: `knowledge hook <verb> --harness codex --pin <version>`, from PATH | A hook runs only once you review it in `/hooks`; the doctor's `codex-trust` warns until then. # Retrieval Protocol

How to find something in this vault **without** reading files. Follow the tiers in order. The point
of the vault is to cut context, and a vault you grep is just a folder.

## The tiers

| # | Tier | Use for | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | The notes the prompt hook adds to each prompt | Breadcrumbs: follow a name into tier 1 or 4 | free |
| 1 | `00-MOC-Root.md` → the `00-MOC-*.md` it points to → the note | "where is X". Most questions end here | ~free |
| 2 | `knowledge find "<q>"` | "what did I write about X" | very low |
| 3 | `knowledge graph <note> [<note>]` | "how does X connect to Y" | very low |
| 4 | `Read` of **one named file** | Only when 1–3 failed | unbounded |

**Stop-check:** about to `Read`, `ls`, `find` or `grep` a vault path without having run tiers 1–3?
That is the violation. Go back to the MOC. If tier 4 was needed, the vault has a gap: fix it.

### 0. Injected notes

The `knowledge` binary searches the vault index on every prompt and adds up to six matching vault
notes, each with a snippet, and the best passage whole when it is short. A snippet is not the note.

### 1. The MOCs

[[00-MOC-Root]] links every folder's `00-MOC-*.md`, and every note is at most two hops from it
([[Conventions]] § Reach). Cheap, current, and it says where things live.

### 2. `knowledge find`: full-text search

The vault index (SQLite FTS5, per machine), from any folder. The question's rarest words rank the
notes; each comes with its best passage. `--json` for scripts, `--limit n` for more than six.

```bash
knowledge find "how does a request reach the cache"
```

`knowledge find "<q>" --repo [<name>]` searches the checkouts' docs, and `--captures` what was kept
or fetched in the last 14 days. Neither is a vault tier.

### 3. `knowledge graph`: relationships

When the question is how notes **connect**, not what they are called: a note's links in and out,
or the shortest path between two, read from the links the index holds.

```bash
knowledge graph Conventions                 # links to, linked from
knowledge graph Conventions Hard-Rules      # the path, up to four links
```

The code map answers the same questions for the checkouts' code: where a symbol is defined, what
uses it, and how two connect. One SQLite file per checkout in the knowledge home, built from each
grammar's own tags query and brought level with git's tracked files before every answer.

```bash
knowledge find <symbol> --code [--repo <name>]   # the definitions, with signatures
knowledge graph <symbol> --code                  # used by, and uses
knowledge graph <symbol> <other> --code          # the path between two
```

### 4. `Read`

Once a tier has **named** the file, `Read` is right: most notes are a few KB. Never a directory
sweep. When a large output will be filtered rather than edited, `<cmd> | knowledge keep "<label>"
--q "<q>"` prints only the matching sections.

## Keeping it honest

An edit reindexes its note at once, and the doctor's `vault-index` check compares the index
with the disk. A write outside Claude (Obsidian, a shell) is picked up by `knowledge index`, which
the daily sweep runs.

| Command | Covers | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `knowledge index` | the vault index: only changed notes are read | **free**, ~1 s for a rebuild |
| `knowledge code index --all` | every checkout's code map: only changed files are parsed | **free** |

**The code map reads git's tracked files only**: a file git ignores or has not been told about is
not in it.

# Why this exists

The reasons behind this vault and its hooks. What each hook does is in [[Hook-Lifecycle]]; how to
use it is in [[README]].

## The problem

Without the vault, every session starts from nothing. The agent re-derives context by reading
files, which is slow, costs context, and yields the same answer each time. Where it does not read,
it falls back on its defaults, and those are often not the owner's: another package manager,
another branching model, a dependency added without a licence check. [[Hard-Rules]] is where each
of those gets written down once.

## The bet

1. **Prime the small, always-true core.** Who the owner is and the rules, imported whole by
   `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, plus what changes per session, injected by the session start (`knowledge hook session`).
2. **Retrieve the long tail.** Everything else is found on demand, cheapest tier first
   ([[Retrieval-Protocol]]): the MOC, then full-text search, then the graph, a file read last.
3. **Capture records automatically.** Sessions, commits and decisions are written by hooks, so
   they exist even when nobody remembers to write them.

## Why hooks, not memory files

Claude Code's own memory is sharded by working directory: what a session learns lands wherever its
terminal happened to be open. A memory the agent must remember to consult, in a place that depends
on the cwd, fails quietly. **A hook runs whether or not the agent remembers to.**

## The failure mode it is designed against: silence

A pipeline like this rarely errors. It goes quiet: a flush that judges everything "nothing worth
keeping", an index that stops matching the vault, a recorder that misses commits, an expired login
behind a background `claude -p`. Each is invisible until someone needs the record. So every part
has a watcher:

| Watch | Catches | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Flush canary | Sessions captured, but no daily note for 3 days | `!! FLUSH CANARY` at session start |
| Failure record | A background `claude -p` that failed, with its reason | `!! BRAIN <TAG> FAILING` at session start |
| `knowledge doctor` | Index, retrieval, sessions, auth, frontmatter, links, reach, ignores, commits, priming, graph, engine links; hygiene as a warning | `knowledge doctor --pretty` |
| Event log | Every capture and what it spawned | `50-Ops/hook-events.jsonl` (gitignored) |
| Daily sweep | `knowledge doctor --repair --record`, once per logical day, detached from the session start | `50-Ops/Health/health-YYYY-MM.md` |
| Health alarm | The sweep's FAIL, or the sweep itself going quiet for 2+ days | `!! VAULT HEALTH` at session start |

## How to know it is working

1. `knowledge doctor --pretty` prints **PASS**.
2. The tail of `50-Ops/Health/health-YYYY-MM.md` shows a PASS line for each recent day.
3. The session start shows **no `!!` lines**. Silence means healthy.

# knowledge: command

A slash command: a skill in `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (user scope, works in every
project) that only you invoke. Since 0.13.1 the engine's own commands are skills of this kind: a
skill is a folder, linked as a junction on Windows, where a `~/.claude/commands/<name>.md` file
link needs Developer Mode.

## Slash-only or model-invoked?

| | Frontmatter | Context cost |
|---|---|---|
| You always type it, deterministic steps | `disable-model-invocation: true` | none until you type it |
| The agent should invoke it on intent | (default) | its description loads into every session |

Default to **slash-only**. A model-invoked skill is a standing tax; this vault deliberately has one
router skill rather than sixteen.

## new

```markdown
---
name: knowledge-<what>
disable-model-invocation: true
description: One line. It is what the / menu shows.
---

Steps, imperative. Reference absolute paths - the skill runs from any cwd.
```

- Name it for what it does: `knowledge-usage`, not `usage`. The folder name is the `/` name.
- `$ARGUMENTS` interpolates what the user typed after the name.
- Keep it short. One that needs 200 lines of instruction wants `references/` beside it.

## edit

On a slash-only skill, `description:` is what the `/` menu shows. On a model-invoked one it decides
when the agent reaches for it, the highest-leverage line in the file: test by asking for the thing
in your own words and seeing whether it fires.

# knowledge: commit

**Delegates.** The `commit-commands:commit` skill already does commits well — use it, then write
the vault side. Do not reimplement commit logic here.

## new

1. Invoke `commit-commands:commit` (or `commit-commands:commit-push-pr` if pushing).
2. Branch the way `00-Meta/Hard-Rules.md` says.
3. Nothing to append by hand: the commit recorder (`knowledge hook post-bash`) writes one note per commit into
   `50-Ops/Commits/`, with the commit body as its reason. A subject-only commit leaves an empty record.
4. If the commit made a decision worth keeping, that is a separate `/knowledge new plan` or an ADR in
   `60-Decisions/<Repo-Name>/` — a commit message is not a decision record.
   ADRs are central, never inside `10-Repos/<repo>/`; the vault gitignores `10-Repos/*/`.

## Scope discipline

Commit only what the task named. If unrelated changes are dirty, leave them unstaged and say so —
do not sweep the user's in-progress work into your commit.

## edit

Amending is for unpushed commits fixing your own noise. Prefer a new commit otherwise.

# knowledge: decision

Record a decision as an ADR, and keep the ledger (`50-Ops/decisions.jsonl`) in step.

## new — a decision made now (tier 1)

1. **Scope.** One repo → `60-Decisions/Repos/<Remote-Name>/`. The vault, its hooks, or how the
   agent must behave → `60-Decisions/Identity/`.
2. **Number** = the highest `NNNN` in that folder + 1. List the folder first; never reuse one.
   The basename must still be unique across the vault — the slug makes it so.
3. **Check it is new.** Search the folder and `00-MOC-Decisions.md`. If this decision already has
   an ADR, **edit that ADR** — two notes for one decision is worse than none.
4. **Write** `<NNNN>-<slug>.md`: frontmatter per `00-Meta/Conventions.md` (`type: decision`,
   `aliases: [ADR-<NNNN>]`), H1 `<NNNN> — <Title>`, then **Decision**, **Why**, **Rejected**
   (alternatives and why not), **Consequences**, **Related** (wikilinks). One decision per file.
5. **Add it** to the table in `60-Decisions/00-MOC-Decisions.md`.
6. **Ledger:** `knowledge note decision "<the decision>" --question "<the question>" --promoted "<vault-relative path>"`

## new --ledger — promote captured answers (tier 2)

1. `knowledge ledger list` — the verbatim questions and chosen answers
   captured from `AskUserQuestion`, with the options that were `offered` and any `note`.
2. Go through them **with the user**, one at a time. For each:
   - a real decision → write the ADR (steps 1–5 above), then
     `knowledge ledger promote <src> "<vault-relative path>"`. The options not chosen are the
     starting point for **Rejected**; ask for the reasons rather than inventing them.
   - several entries that are one decision → one ADR, promote each `src` to the same path
   - not a decision (a preference already recorded, a one-off) →
     `knowledge ledger promote <src> not-a-decision`
3. The captured answer is the user's literal choice — quote it; do not reword what they chose.

# knowledge: docs

A reusable knowledge note. Not repo-specific — anything tied to one repo belongs in that repo's
`docs/`, not here.

## new

1. **Category** → `20-Knowledge/{Rust,Tauri,Case-Studies,Web,Tooling}/`. If none fit, ask before
   inventing a new folder — that is `/knowledge new structure`.
2. **Filename** kebab-case, `.md`. Existing numbered notes keep their prefixes.
3. **Frontmatter:**

```yaml
---
type: doc
tags: [rust, tauri]          # required, lowercase
aliases: [Alt Name]          # optional, how else you'd search for it
created: <today>
updated: <today>
status: active
---
```

4. **Body.** One concept per note. If it needs two MOC entries, it is two notes.
   Lead with what the reader needs, not with background. Code blocks over prose where the code
   is the answer.
5. **Link it from `20-Knowledge/00-MOC-Knowledge.md`** under its category. A note missing from the
   MOC is unreachable at retrieval tier 1.
6. Add `[[wikilinks]]` to related notes. Dangling links are fine — they mark future notes.

## edit

- Bump `updated:`. Never touch `created:`.
- Preserve `prev:`/`next:`/`parent:` chains — the migrated notes use them for learning paths.
- Superseding: set `status: superseded` on the old note and link forward to the replacement.
  Do not delete; the links pointing at it still resolve.
- Renaming breaks nothing (Obsidian resolves by name) but check the MOC entry still matches.

# knowledge: hook

**Delegates.** The `update-config` skill owns `settings.json` — hooks, permissions, env. Use it.

## new

1. Invoke `update-config` with what should fire and when.
2. **Preserve existing hooks.** `~/.claude/settings.json` already holds the engine's hooks and
   possibly a plugin's. Add to the `hooks` object; never overwrite it.
3. The engine's hooks are `knowledge hook <event>`, carried by its plugin. A hook of your own
   lives outside the skeleton checkout, so a skeleton pull never overwrites it.
4. Document what it does in `20-Knowledge/Tooling/`, or it becomes unexplainable magic in six months.

## Keep hooks small

A hook fires on every matching event in every project. Anything slow or chatty is felt constantly.
One line of output, or none.

## edit

Disabling: remove the entry from `settings.json`, keep the script. Deleting the script makes a
stale reference fail loudly on every session start.

# knowledge: plan

**Delegates.** Plan mode already writes plans to `~/.claude/plans/*.md`. Harvest those — do not
re-author from memory.

## new

1. Find the source: `~/.claude/plans/` for a plan-mode plan, or the conversation.
2. **Where it goes — always the vault**, one repo or many (user instruction, 2026-09-20):
   `40-Plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md` — a folder note, never `plan.md`: every
   basename in the vault is unique. Beside it as needed: `YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>-spec.md`,
   `-implementation.md`, `stages/`, `evidence/`. Never inside a checkout.
3. Frontmatter `type: plan`, `status: draft`, and `project: <repo>` when it concerns one repo.
4. Keep the **Context** section — why, not just what. A plan without its reasoning is unreviewable
   six months later.
5. Run `knowledge hubs` so it appears in `40-Plans/00-MOC-Plans.md`.

## edit — recording the outcome

This is the part that gets skipped and is worth the most.

- `status: active` while executing, `complete` when done, `superseded` when replaced.
- Add an **Outcome** section: what actually happened, what the plan got wrong, what you'd do
  differently. A plan with no outcome teaches nothing on re-read.
- Findings that outlived the plan get promoted to a `20-Knowledge/` note and linked.

# knowledge: repo

A thin pointer page in `10-Repos/` carrying the completion-gate `status`, or a whole new project.

## new — page for an existing repo

The repo's own `docs/` is its documentation. This page is an **index**, never a copy.

```yaml
---
type: repo
project: <slug>
tags: [...]
aliases: [Other Name]        # if the folder name differs from the project name
created: <today>
updated: <today>
status: in-progress          # completion gate reads this
checkout: <Remote-Name>      # relative to devRoot; the doctor's pointers check resolves it per machine
docs: <Remote-Name>/docs     # optional, same rule
---
```

Never an absolute path in `checkout:`/`docs:`: the checkouts folder differs per machine, and
the doctor's `pointers` check fails on one.

Sections that earn their place:
- What it is, and **where the code is** (path, remote, branch, license)
- **Its own docs** — a table pointing into the repo, not restating it
- Stack, compared against the other repos where that comparison is informative
- **Known gaps — don't chase these** ← the highest-value section. Stops re-investigation of
  things already decided against.

Then link from `10-Repos/00-MOC-Repos.md`.

## Always — the asset folder

Every repo gets `80-Assets/Repos/<Repo-Name>/`, named exactly as the `10-Repos/` directory:

```bash
mkdir -p "80-Assets/Repos/<Repo-Name>" && touch "80-Assets/Repos/<Repo-Name>/.gitkeep"
```

Masters only — the `.svg` a logo is drawn in, the source of a README banner, the icon set an

## Before creating anything

Ask: does this belong in an existing folder? A new top-level directory is almost always wrong.
`20-Knowledge/` takes new *categories* readily; the numbered top level does not grow casually.

## new

1. Name it to sort correctly. Numbered top-level (`00-`…`90-`) is reserved and full;
   `20-Knowledge/` subfolders are plain PascalCase or single words.
2. Create `00-MOC-<Scope>.md` immediately — a folder without a MOC is invisible at retrieval tier 1:

## edit — reorganising

- Moving notes is safe: Obsidian resolves wikilinks by **name**, not path.
- What *does* break: MOC link lists, and the path rules in `.gitignore` and `.obsidian/app.json`
  (`knowledge doctor`'s `ignores` check names a stale one).
- After any move, re-run the link check and `knowledge index`.

# knowledge: task

Uses the `obsidian-tasks-plugin` format already installed in the vault. Do not invent a syntax.

## new

Tasks live in today's daily note, `30-Sessions/YYYY/MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`.
**Rollover is `rolloverHour` local time** (config, default 5) — with the default, a session starting
02:00 belongs to the previous day's note.

```markdown
- [ ] Fix the labeler.yml v5 schema [[my-app]] 📅 2026-08-22 ⏫
```

- `[[wikilink]]` the repo or note it belongs to — that is what makes it findable later
- `📅 YYYY-MM-DD` due · `⏫` high `🔼` medium `🔽` low · `🔁` recurring
- One action per task. "Fix CI" is not a task; "rewrite labeler.yml in v5 schema" is.

## edit

- Complete: `- [x]` with `✅ YYYY-MM-DD`. The plugin queries on this.
- Reschedule: change `📅`, don't delete and recreate — you lose the link context.
- A task open for weeks is either not a task or not real. Say so rather than rescheduling silently.

# People MOC

The people the owner knows and helps: colleagues, classmates, friends, clients. **Check this page
before doing something for someone.** Their note records who they are, what they know, what they
like and how they write, so the work fits them without asking the owner again.

## People

## How this folder works

- **One folder per person:** `People/<first-last>/<first-last>.md`, `type: person`, kebab-case
  ASCII (transliterate accented letters, so `ğ` becomes `g` and `ü` becomes `u`). The identity note
  is the folder note. Notes about the person can sit beside it. Work made *for* them stays with the
  work (a plan folder, a repo) and their note links to it.
- **When the owner introduces someone new, add their folder** and a row in the table above.
- **What a note holds:**
  - who they are to the owner
  - basics: age, school, work
  - what they know
  - what they like: design, tone
  - how they write
  - what has been done for them
  - what is still unknown
- **Only what the owner said or what their own material shows.** Mark a derived fact as derived
  (an age turned into a birth year, say). Ask the owner rather than guess.
- **Private.** Nobody's data goes into a public repo, a public page, or a commit outside the vault.
  Check that the vault's own remote is private before adding anyone.
- **Pronouns:** use the ones the owner uses for that person. If the owner hasn't said, use they/them.
  Never infer pronouns from a name.
